title: CATL begins test production of battery cells in Debrecen - electrive.com
content:
Chinese battery giant CATL has begun test production of battery cells at its new plant in Debrecen, Hungary. Previously, there were multiple delays, forcing European automakers to source supplies from China as an alternative. More recently, political headwinds have also emerged.
Aerial view of the new CATL factory in Debrecen
Image: CATL
CATL has begun test production at its new battery cell plant in Debrecen, Hungary. According to the company, this follows the successful fulfilment of all necessary prerequisites and regulatory requirements. The test phase aims to fully set up, optimise, and validate the production facilities and manufacturing processes before mass production begins. The first two production lines at the plant have now been commissioned for these test purposes.
However, it remains unclear when full-scale mass production of battery cells in Debrecen will actually commence. Test production in new cell factories typically lasts months rather than weeks. On the other hand, CATL is the world’s largest battery cell manufacturer, with extensive experience in the field. Its customers are eagerly awaiting the cells: according to a media report, Mercedes-Benz
even had to halt
production of the all-electric GLC in Bremen this summer because CATL was unable to supply enough cells. In response, the company specifically restructured its supply chain to
temporarily supply Mercedes with cells from China
for the GLC and VLE.
CATL already operates a cell factory in Thuringia
CATL announced the Debrecen plant
in August 2022
as its second European cell factory, alongside the facility in Arnstadt, Thuringia, which opened at the end of 2022. The plan included investments of €7.34 billion and a production capacity of up to 100 GWh per year, making it CATL’s largest factory outside China. The Debrecen plant is set to supply locally produced cells to Mercedes-Benz, as well as BMW – which
also operates its new EV factory in Debrecen
– and other European automakers. Construction of the first phase began in 2023, but the originally expected production start was delayed several times; it was
supposed to begin in spring 2026
Additional challenges arose during the ramp-up, including approval and environmental issues. Local residents and environmental organisations contested the environmental permits, with experts criticising aspects such as water consumption, noise, and impacts on the water balance. This summer, a non-compliant wastewater discharge and elevated
nickel exposure among employees
led to regulatory interventions. While
production of battery modules had already begun
, cell manufacturing took longer to get underway.
The project also faces an increasingly critical political environment: the government of Viktor Orbán, which was voted out in April, had heavily supported Hungary’s development into a European battery hub and attracted several Asian manufacturers to the country. Following the change in government, the new leadership under Prime Minister Péter Magyar
announced stricter environmental controls and new oversight for the battery industry
. However, there is no clear evidence of a direct link between the political shift and the delays at CATL; the company emphasises that it has obtained the necessary approvals for the now-launched trial operation and has rectified the previously identified deficiencies.

title: EVE Open Source Battery™: AI Battery Debuts at IAA TRANSPORTATION 2026 - electrive.com
content:
HANNOVER, Germany, Sept. 19, 2026 – Amid accelerating global electrification, EVE Open Source Battery™ 4.0: AI Battery made its European debut at IAA TRANSPORTATION 2026. The booth showcased EVE Energy’s system-level product advantages and localised European operational capabilities. Attracting extensive visits from leading global enterprises for in-depth exchanges, EVE secured strategic cooperation orders exceeding 30 GWh on-site.
Image: EVE Energy
Rooted in robust product performance and an open ecosystem philosophy, EVE Energy continues to expand its European commercial vehicle market footprint and advance low-carbon transition across global transportation sectors.
EVE AI Battery: Redefining the Operational Value for Global Commercial Vehicles
At IAA TRANSPORTATION under the theme “Mighty Battery, Mighty Mind”, EVE exhibited Open Source Battery 3.0 and 4.0: AI Battery solutions. The lineup features cutting-edge LMX chemistry cells including LM815, LM285 and V63, alongside the
LM815-641kWh
underfloor battery system for heavy-duty trucks and the B3E-LF206S battery system for buses. Featuring high capacity, lightweight design, extended cycle life and superior low-temperature performance, this lineup stood out prominently at the booth.
At its core, the EVE’s LMX chemical material retains the high safety and stability inherent to LFP material, while pushing energy-density limits and significantly enhancing low-temperature performance. The products fully comply with stringent European market access requirements and adapt to complex, harsh operating environments, addressing key pain points for commercial vehicle electrification across the region.
Built upon this advanced material platform, EVE Open Source Battery™ 4.0: AI Battery marks a major leap forward in battery intelligence. Integrated with a custom-built AI chip, it enables cell-level active sensing, real-time diagnostics and intelligent optimisation, transforming conventional passive battery management systems. With full perception, deep reasoning and self-evolution capabilities, the solution elevates battery management to safeguard safe, efficient and reliable operation of commercial vehicle batteries.
Product Launch: Unveiling the Proven Capabilities of EVE Open Source Battery
At IAA TRANSPORTATION, EVE Energy hosted a dedicated product launch — “EVE Open Source Battery™ 4.0: AI Battery — The New Era of Global Commercial Transportation” — for visiting commercial vehicle OEMs, value-chain partners and industry media. The event presented the brand proposition of Open Source Battery. Guided by European regulatory standards and operational challenges across complex cross-regional scenarios, EVE outlined the product value, LMX chemistry and technical strengths of its solutions. Through open and collaborative industrial dialogue, EVE explored viable commercial vehicle electrification pathways with attendees, underscoring the robust overseas deployment potential of its Open Source Battery series.
Partnering with Global Partners to Usher in New Chapters of Collaboration
Throughout IAA TRANSPORTATION, EVE Energy’s booth drew broad attention from global industry stakeholders, with vibrant on-site exchanges. Leading commercial vehicle OEMs (such as BAIC, SANY, Nivalis), core value-chain partners and international mainstream media visited the booth for in-depth, pragmatic discussions covering European commercial vehicle electrification trends, extreme-condition optimisation and localised deployment partnerships. This close alignment of requirements fully validates global market recognition of EVE Energy’s technical innovation strengths and premium product lineup.
Backed by robust technological innovation, reliable product performance and global service capabilities,
EVE Energy
achieved fruitful outcomes at the exhibition. The company signed on-site cooperation agreements with high-calibre industry players including BMZ, Janus Electric, Morris Commercial, Sunswap, WEG and others, with total contracted orders exceeding 30 GWh. These deals highlighted global stakeholders’ strong trust and recognition of EVE Open Source Battery solutions, leading-edge technologies and comprehensive delivery capabilities.
Deepening its global footprint and co-building an electrified ecosystem, open collaboration underpins EVE Energy’s globalisation strategy. Looking ahead, the company will steadily advance technological innovation and product upgrades. Aligning its diversified, highly adaptable product portfolio with regional market demands worldwide, EVE will deepen multi-dimensional synergies with global value-chain partners and accelerate the electrification, intelligence and decarbonisation of commercial vehicles globally — injecting strong momentum into the sustainable development of the global transport sector.

title: Korea opens ‘new Silk Road’ to battery tech partnerships in Central Asia   – Batteries International
content: South Korea’s president has put materials critical to the battery industry and manufacturing technology at the centre of what he called a ‘new Silk Road’ pact with Central Asian nations. Lee Jae-myung used the first Korea-Central Asia Business Summit on September 16 to call for a move beyond raw materials trade and strengthen “full-cycle cooperation” in the critical minerals sector — covering exploration, smelting, high-value material processing and final product production. Leaders from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz, Tajikstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan took part in the one-day summit, during which a total of 19 memoranda of understanding relating to business cooperation were signed. One of the agreements, between the Korea Institute of Industrial Technology and Kazakhstan’s national institute for metallurgical and ore research, set out a blueprint for mineral supply chain cooperation by “linking local resources with domestic technology”. Lee said: “As global supply chains are being reorganised, Central Asia is a treasure trove of essential critical minerals for electric vehicles, batteries, and semiconductor production.” When abundant resources such as lithium meets Korean manufacturing capabilities, partner nations can lead the global market, he said. “Korean companies with extensive construction experience and proven technology are the best partners to innovate Central Asia’s infrastructure. We must build transportation and energy arteries connecting vast continents, along with a dense logistics network, to unlock Eurasia’s potential.” The summit comes as Korea strives to challenge China’s dominance of the global battery sector by building international alliances. Batteries International reported last year that Korea had scrambled to shore up the country’s faltering battery sector with an initial cash infusion worth close to $15 billion, as a global slump in EV sales took its toll on the industry. Earlier this year, a Korean joint venture including battery material and chemicals group Posco Future M broke ground for an LFP cathode materials plant in the country targeting the ESS and EV batteries market. That came after US battery tech company Coreshell Technologies agreed an eight-year LFP supply deal with Korea’s L&F Corporation in a move to offer a “fully China-free” battery materials option. title: $7bn US ‘super smelter’ project clears environmental hurdle – Batteries International
content: Plans for a US-based super smelter to boost domestic supply of critical materials, including lead, have cleared a major regulatory hurdle. The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) confirmed on September 11 it had adopted a finding of no significant impact in terms of upgrades to its transmission system to support the Project Crucible development in Montgomery County. Batteries International revealed in December 2025 that Korea Zinc was partnering the US government to build the smelter, at a total investment cost of $7.4 billion, after lead was added to the nation’s list of critical minerals. The US war department was the lead federal agency for the environmental review, with TVA serving as a cooperating agency. TVA said the finding also addresses its view that another review is not required. The war department is considering financial support for the construction and operation of the facility by Crucible Metals near Clarksville — at the site of the existing Crucible Zinc plant. Under the proposal, TVA would provide up to 230MW of additional load to the facility, which would require new infrastructure and several upgrades to the transmission system near the project site. Full power availability is anticipated in 2029. Project Crucible is a proposed integrated non-ferrous smelting and refining facility intended to produce 12 types of non-ferrous metals, including 11 of the 60 critical minerals designated by the US government, as well as semiconductor-grade sulfuric acid. Products include zinc, lead, copper, gold, antimony, gallium and germanium. The project has been designated as ‘FAST-41’ — a federal classification reserved for major infrastructure projects requiring enhanced inter-agency coordination. Project Crucible moved ahead last April following Korea Zinc’s acquisition of Nyrstar assets in the US. Korea Zinc said previously construction of the smelter would begin with site preparation in 2026, followed by phased commercial operations from 2029. The facility is expected to process more than one million tonnes of raw materials annually and produce a total of 540,000 tonnes of finished products. Design of the smelter will be based on Korea Zinc’s Onsan facility in Ulsan, which the company said is the world’s largest single-site smelter by production capacity, using world-leading smelting technology, optimal processes, and state-of-the-art control systems. title: Birla Carbon cites ‘geopolitical instability’ in 15% price hike – Batteries International
content: Birla Carbon has announced a price increase of up to 15% for its speciality materials products in Asia from October 1. The carbon additives group said the increase was needed to counter what the company said were significant and sustained increases in feedstock costs, driven in part by geopolitical instability and disruptions in global feedstock markets. The announcement comes just three months after Batteries International reported the group was embarking on a global business shake-up to focus on expansion in Asia in the face of weakened demand in the Americas and Europe. Birla said then it was continuing to assess its asset base in line with market trends, as it moved to a structure focused on three business units — Asia, Americas & EMEA and specialty materials. On the price increase, Birla said it has been working to mitigate the impact of the increases through operational efficiencies, supply chain optimisation and disciplined cost management: “However, the magnitude and duration of the cost escalation have made a price adjustment necessary.” In 2023, the group acquired carbon nanotube firm Nanocyl to strengthen its presence in the lithium battery materials sector. Earlier this year, Birla said it had secured a €2 million ($2.3 million) grant to boost energy autonomy at its plant in Spain. The grant from the Society for Regional Development of Cantabria formed part of a broader investment project by the firm aimed at strengthening energy self-sufficiency at the facility. title: GM Launches Closed-Loop EV Battery Recycling Pilot Program
content:
Battery Recycling
EV Batteries
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Automotive & Mobility
Industry Trends
Learn about GM’s closed-loop battery recycling program, its meaning, advantages, and how it supports sustainable EV production.
September 22, 2026
4 Min Read
A GMC Sierra EV with battery cells made from recycled materials rolls off the line at GM’s Factory ZERO assembly facility.
Courtesy of Cirba Solutions.
Lithium-ion batteries power electric vehicles (EVs) and contain
critical minerals
that are highly valued in the battery supply chain. However, extracting and processing these materials comes with significant environmental and ethical challenges. To address these concerns, automotive companies are increasingly adopting and improving battery recycling methods; one is closed-loop battery recycling, a sustainable approach that promises to transform the EV battery lifecycle.
What is closed-loop battery recycling?
Closed-loop battery recycling is a circular system in which end-of-life batteries are collected, dismantled, and processed to recover valuable critical minerals. These recovered minerals are then reintroduced into the manufacturing of new batteries, creating a self-sustaining cycle. Unlike traditional recycling methods, closed-loop systems aim to retain the integrity of critical minerals, ensuring they can be reused in high-performance applications.
Related:
What Is Black Mass in Lithium-Ion Batteries?
Why are automotive companies embracing closed-loop recycling?
Environmental sustainability
: The extraction of critical minerals like lithium and cobalt is energy-intensive and environmentally damaging. Mining operations often lead to deforestation, water pollution, and significant carbon emissions. By recycling batteries, car manufacturers can reduce their reliance on critical minerals, thereby minimizing the environmental footprint of EV production.
Cost efficiency
: As the demand for EVs grows, so does the cost of critical minerals. Closed-loop recycling offers a cost-effective alternative by recovering and reusing materials that would otherwise be discarded. This not only reduces production costs but also protects car manufacturers from volatile raw material markets.
Regulatory compliance
: Governments worldwide are introducing stricter regulations to ensure responsible disposal and recycling of EV batteries. For instance, the
European Union’s Battery Regulation
mandates that a certain percentage of materials in new batteries must come from recycled sources. By adopting closed-loop systems, car manufacturers can stay ahead of regulatory requirements and avoid potential penalties.
Brand reputation
: Modern consumers are increasingly conscious of the environmental impact of the products they purchase. Car manufacturers that adopt sustainable practices, such as closed-loop recycling, can enhance their brand image and appeal to eco-conscious buyers.
GM closed-loop battery recycling pilot program
General Motors (GM) has announced its new approach to sustainable EV production with the launch of a closed-loop battery recycling pilot program. This initiative, shared by Kurt Kelty, GM’s Vice President of Battery and Sustainability, highlights the company’s efforts to reduce the carbon footprint of battery materials while addressing cost challenges. Kelty described the program as “a pathway for using recovered battery materials in new cells” and emphasized its role in supporting GM’s broader goals of sustainability and affordability.
Related:
What Really Happens to Spent EV Batteries?
GM’s collaborative effort and industry implications
The pilot's success required years of engineering, quality assurance, logistics, testing, and manufacturing work across GM and its partners. Collaborators such as Cirba Solutions, Ultium Cells, LG Energy Solution, and others played a critical role in ensuring the program’s success.
As part of the pilot, GM collaborated with
Cirba Solutions
to recover 80 end-of-life GM EV batteries. These batteries were processed into black mass—a blend of critical minerals such as nickel, cobalt, and manganese — and used to create cathode active material (CAM). GM’s partners converted the black mass into over 12 metric tons of cathode active material made entirely from recycled nickel, cobalt, and manganese.
Related:
7 Battery Recycling Companies Scaling Up in North America in 2026
“Battery recycling is an important, intersecting component across the battery supply chain, and this program effectively demonstrates the value that recycling end-of-life batteries brings to creating a closed-loop supply of critical minerals,” stated David Klanecky, President and CEO of Cirba Solutions.
Display of reclaimed materials/elements, including black mass from recycled EV Lithium batteries. Courtesy of John Keeble / Contributor/Getty Images Europe.
GM’s real-world application
GM stated that it validated this new cathode active material to the same high standards for quality, safety, and performance required for use in an EV. Once validated, the pilot program’s success was demonstrated when GM produced its first EVs powered by battery cells containing 100% recycled nickel, cobalt, and manganese. Vehicles such as the Cadillac LYRIQ, Chevrolet Silverado EV Trail Boss, and GMC Sierra EV AT4 were assembled at Factory ZERO and Spring Hill Assembly using these recycled materials.

title: VW ID.3 GTI Concept Delivers 321 Horsepower
content:
Automotive & Mobility

The battery-electric hot hatch delivers rear-wheel drive and 5.6-second 0-62 mph acceleration with 375-mile range.
September 22, 2026
6 Slides
Start slideshow
Volkswagen ID.3 GTI concept
Volkswagen
At a Glance
The ID.3 GTI concept features 321 horsepower, making it the most powerful GTI ever produced.
VW's electric hot hatch switches to rear-wheel drive, departing from traditional front-drive GTIs.
The concept achieves 375 miles of range with a 79-kWh battery and 183-kW DC fast charging capability.
Since its debut at the 1975
Frankfurt Motor Show
Volkswagen’s GTI
has been synonymous with practical performance. Increasingly, practicality demands electric drive, so VW is previewing its notion of a future battery-electric GTI with the ID.3 GTI concept.
The company terms this as a “near-production concept vehicle,” and so far is non-committal about the US market, telling
Design News
in an email, "The ID.3 GTI is an exciting example of the momentum behind Volkswagen's global EV strategy. While we have no news to share for the U.S. at this time, we're working hard to ensure the EVs we bring to America are the right fit for our customers, and we're optimistic about the future of our electric lineup."
ID.3 is VW’s battery-electric model
that corresponds in size to its Golf compact hatchback that served as the platform for the very first GTI. Over the decades, VW has applied the GTI badge to a variety of models, such as the subcompact Polo, and has already introduced the all-electric ID.Polo GTI.
Related:
Revoy's Electric Mini-Trailer Cuts Diesel Truck Fuel Use by Up to 90% With Battery Swaps
But an important difference is that while the ID.Polo GTI adheres to VW’s past practice of front-drive GTI hot hatches, the ID.3 GTI is proposed as a rear-drive model. The ID.3 GTI packs a 321-horsepower version of VW’s APP550 drive unit, making it the most powerful GTI model in the brand’s history.
This produces 0-62 mph acceleration in 5.6 seconds. DC fast-charging is somewhat slower, with a claimed 10% to 80% state of charge time of half an hour at a peak rate of 183 kilowatts. The 79-kilowatt-hour battery pack is good for 375 miles of driving range, according to VW.
The company is proud to show a new 12.9-inch display for its new Innovision infotainment system, which can only be an improvement on the company’s current infotainment product. One step forward is the inclusion of a row of physical buttons below the display for HVAC controls and a console-mounted rotary volume knob with up and down tuning/track advance buttons.
Those are the only details available from this teaser, but there seems little reason to doubt the ID.3 GTI will go into production and will probably come to the US, barring any additional unforeseen obstacles to international trade from the government.

title: Bridewell Explores Vulnerabilities in the Aviation Industry
content:
Bridewell Explores Vulnerabilities in the Aviation Industry
Prioritise Us
on Google
Ongoing cyber attacks are putting aviation supply chains at risk. Credit: Getty
Kelechi Onyedebelu, Director of Cybersecurity Solutions at Bridewell explores the growing risk for aviation supply chains following ongoing cyber attacks
The rise of technology has meant great things for global supply chains, bringing in new levels of efficiency and reducing fragmentation risks.
However, the growing reliance on digital tools and AI have also put supply chains at a greater risk of cyber attacks.
The aviation industry is one of the many which has been impacted by this change. Bridewell, a cyber security partner, has released a report exploring the supply chain impact of cyber attacks on the aviation industry.
A changing environment
Digital innovation is revolutionary for how modern supply chains operate, faced by an increased pressure to do more, act faster and spend less money. While this is a significant benefit for organisations, it also means they have increased points of entry into their data bases.
Over the past year,
cyber attacks
have been hitting the news, resulting in mass data breaches and operations shutting down.
The aviation industry has seen significant changes over the past two decades, becoming increasingly dependent on interconnected digital systems as it modernises and gains greater efficiency.
“This increased interconnectivity has brought massive improvements for airlines, airports and passengers. Airlines and airports operate more efficiently, sophisticated systems help manage growing demand, and data can be shared in real time,” explains Kelechi Onyedebelu, Director Security Solutions Presales at Bridewell US.
“However, this also widens the attack surface, creating more opportunities for cyber criminals to exploit.  Airlines, airports,
manufacturers
and suppliers now all operate on interconnected technologies so cyber resilience cannot be achieved by individual organisations working in isolation.”
Report findings
US$1,433,059 - the mean losses from an attack or breach
100% of respondents said they experienced financial losses due to a breach in the last year
In the past 12 months, 46% of respondents have seen an increase in attacks against their organisation
30% of the attack entry points was caused by compromised credentials
Malware, credential theft and DDOS attacks were experienced by 8% of respondents
On average, an organisation experienced 3.85 phishing attacks in the last year
More than ¾ respondents have seen organisational increases to cybersecurity budgets in the current fiscal year
Kelechi Onyedebelu, Director Security Solutions Presales at Bridewell US
Supply chain risk
To investigate the impact of attacks on the industry, Bridewell surveyed 250 cybersecurity professionals in the aviation industry. Though attacks have become more innovative, the report finds that the main issue is caused by the frequency of which they are occurring.
Almost half of the respondents state that the volume of attacks against their organisations has increased in the last 12 months, which coincides with the rapid digitalisation of supply chains.
The most common entry point for attacks was through
compromised credentials
, as reported by 30% of respondents. Alongside this, as high as 13.2% stated that third-party and supply chain access was an entry point for these attacks.
This occurs as third parties have weaker security systems, so are targeted by the hackers. Once the hackers are in the suppliers or vendors systems, they have an indirect pathway into the larger organisation’s defences, allowing them access to the entire data base, client list, partner ecosystem and more.
The aviation industry is under sustained pressure and experiencing significant financial losses as a result.
Kelechi Onyedebelu, Director Security Solutions Presales at Bridewell US
Manchester Airports Group (MAG), which owns Manchester, East Midlands and London Stansted airports, was hit by a cyberattack and stolen data was published | Credit: Manchester Airports Group
The wider impact
In August 2026, the
Manchester Airports Group
revealed that it had been victim to a major data breach, with personal information of more than 8.5 million individuals compromised. This group operates Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports.
Data was harvested from customers who had signed up for terminal Wi-Fi, airport parking, lounge access or Fast Track security passes, demonstrating how a hyper-connected ecosystem reveals major vulnerabilities in the network.
Aviation groups have increasingly seen attacks, which result in major data breaches and financial losses – caused by delays, reputational damage and disruption.
Bridewell found that 100% of respondents were financially impacted by an attack, with 45.2% describing their most significant attack as having a critical or high impact on their organisation.
“What weʼre seeing is that the aviation industry is under sustained pressure and experiencing significant financial losses as a result,” Kelechi continues.
“As artificial intelligence, automation and increasingly connected infrastructure continue to reshape aviation, understanding the industryʼs cyber maturity is essential.”
According to the report, 70.8% of respondents have adopted AI or machine learning as a tool for cyber defence, and 77.6% have seen
increased budgets
for cybersecurity within their organisation.
With increased supply chain complexity, comes increased risk. The last 12 months have demonstrated exactly how vulnerable organisations are to attacks, meaning investments need to be made to
increase resilience
and protect assets.

HQ: Manchester, UK
Manchester Airports Group (MAG), the UK's largest airport operator, owns Manchester, London Stansted, and East Midlands airports plus digital travel business CAVU. Criminal hackers breached MAG systems and posted personal data of 8.5 million people online after their unpaid ransom demand failed.

It halted production at UK sites in Solihull, Halewood, and Wolverhampton while IT teams managed complex recovery efforts.

title: How ITC & DHL Support Small Businesses in Cross-Border Trade
content:
How ITC & DHL Support Small Businesses in Cross-Border Trade
Prioritise Us
on Google
The International Trade Centre (ITC) and DHL have signed a new memorandum of understanding to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Credit: Getty Images
Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director of the International Trade Centre, says its DHL partnership will help SMEs overcome cross-border trade barriers
The International Trade Centre (ITC) and DHL have signed a new memorandum of understanding to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
DHL and the ITC’s partnership dates back to 2016, with a focus on supporting
women-led businesses
in cross-border trades.
Through the renewed agreement, ITC’s market intelligence and trade expertise will be available to DHL’s global logistics network.
It aims to help SMEs overcome the barriers that continue to keep many of them out of international markets.
"For small businesses, the main challenge is not in creating quality products for customers but getting it to them," says Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director at ITC.
Key Facts: ITC-DHL Partnership Renewal
Partnership between ITC and DHL dates back to 2016
DHL GoTrade has reached more than 26,000 SMEs since 2021
ITC SheTrades has supported more than 4,000 women-led businesses
ecomConnect connected 400+ SMEs with DHL support between 2020-2024
Some markets saw shipping costs cut by up to 60% through the partnership
Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director of ITC, and Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa, sign a Memorandum of Understanding renewing the ITC-DHL partnership. Credit: DHL Group
Inside the ITC-DHL trade partnership
Under the renewed agreement, ITC and DHL will support small businesses across exports,
supply chains and logistics
The partnership will work with business support organisations and ITC SheTrades Hubs to strengthen services for small and women-led companies.
SMEs and women entrepreneurs will also receive support in international trade discussions among private-sector and government bodies.
DHL says SMEs account for around 90% of businesses globally, provide roughly 70% of employment and contribute around 70% of global GDP.
Despite this, many continue to face barriers when attempting to fully participate in international trade.
Over the past decade, ITC and DHL have worked together through DHL GoTrade, ITC SheTrades and the ITC ecomConnect programme, reaching small businesses in more than 60
countries across Africa
, ASEAN, Latin America and the Caribbean.
Since 2021, GoTrade has supported more than 26,000 SMEs and 8,000 women-owned businesses.
EcomConnect linked more than 400 SMEs with DHL support between 2020 and 2024, including shipping arrangements that cut costs by up to 60% in some markets.
We're deepening our work with DHL to help more small businesses, particularly women-led businesses
Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director at ITC
Closing the SME finance gap
Logistics access is not the only barrier for SMEs trying to
trade internationally
, as access to finance remains a significant constraint.
The partnership specifically targets this issue for women-led businesses, as they traditionally face issues around funding.
According to the World Bank and International Finance Corporation's most recent MSME Finance Gap Report, SMEs across 119 emerging markets and developing economies face a combined financing shortfall of around US$5.7tn.
The report found that 40% of formal MSMEs are credit-constrained, with women-owned businesses alone accounting for approximately US$1.9tn of that gap.
Pamela says: “We're deepening our work with DHL to help more small businesses, particularly women-led businesses, to overcome
last-mile logistics
barriers and reach new markets and to ensure their perspectives are heard at decision-making tables.”
Initiatives like GoTrade and SheTrades represent a narrower, logistics-focused intervention within a far larger structural problem.
ITC and DHL’s agreement aims to address the financing gap, while reducing other obstacles standing between SMEs and the international markets.

DHL Group is the world's leading express logistics and postal company, delivering global supply chain solutions, parcel delivery and international trade freight services. Driving connectivity across international markets, the organisation actively advances automated warehousing, digitised tracking networks and sustainable low-emission transport infrastructure.

on Google

As the global trade environment becomes increasingly complex and more competitive, ImportGenius CEO Michael Kanko positions ImportGenius as a critical tool
Global supply chains are facing ongoing challenges and an increasingly competitive market.
As sustainability, speed and digitalisation increase in priorities – alongside
long-term resilience
– new organisations are emerging ready to fill the gap in the market.
In today’s world, choice is crucial, but it can be overwhelming for decision-makers.
Almost two decades ago, ImportGenius was founded in order to make global trade data transparent – now, it has expanded significantly and is working to revolutionise trade intelligence.
Organisation expansion
ImportGenius was founded in 2007, making headlines in 2008 when it discovered that
was preparing to launch the iPhone 3G. This occurred when it used its customs data to uncover 188 unrecorded containers that were shipped by Apple and its logistics partners.
Since then, the company has become a trusted data source for large-scale news outlets, has scaled its solutions to help global enterprises and has continuously expanded its operations into new markets.
Today, ImportGenius is working on transforming trade intelligence by using AI and other digital tools to enhance supply chain visibility. It collects, organises and makes information from the international trade industry accessible. Through this, it helps clients understand
shipping manifests
and customs records in order to make informed decisions with confidence.
It connects fragmented data and turns it into actionable information, helping readers find their ideal supplier, track market shifts and
navigate global trade
Key stats
3.3 billion+ shipments are recorded through ImportGenius
The company has insights into shipment-level records across more than 25 countries
ImportGenius has served more than 50K businesses
More than 8 million US importers are tracked
There is shipment data on more than 16 million importers and exporters around the world
ImportGenius can offer shipment-level insights into global trade (Credit: Getty Images)
Supply chain impact
In 2025, ImportGenius launched GlobalPro, its annual subscription service which offers enterprise-level access to US trade data, which is updated daily. This means there was more thorough visibility into global trade, faster time-to-value for sourcing and logistics teams and a greater depth of coverage.
As tariffs and
supply chain volatility
became a major concern for organisations in 2025, this service came at a crucial period. This level of insight into competitors and their international clients helped increase clarity for decision-makers. As new trade lanes were being established and cross-border strategies were becoming more complex, this data helped increase cohesion across data sets.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, 50% of US businesses close within five years, and 65% close within a decade.
ImportGenius CEO Michael Kanko points to a decline in competitiveness as a core reason. There are large numbers of competitors, but they lack the information to drive them into more innovative action.
ImportGenius, therefore, aims to increase this competitiveness by offering succinct data points about global supply chains. The increased level in transparency and cohesion helps drive business decisions and also influences wider
industry policy
We didn’t just create a tool: we created an entirely new way for businesses to see the world. Our data has changed supply chains, influenced policy and made businesses better and safer.
Founder & CEO of ImportGenius, Michael Kanko
Founder & CEO of ImportGenius, Michael Kanko. Credit: ImportGenius
ImportGenius, therefore, is helping organisations turn trade data into sourcing intelligence and supply chain analytics, offering shipment-level intelligence which provides strong market insights for supplier relationship management. Through this, clients can gain verified information on potential suppliers, market risk and sourcing opportunities.

Prioritise Us

Tzar Taraporvala and Smayan Mehra, Founders of Anchr. Credit: Anchr
AI operating system Anchr is modernising the critical food distribution industry following the raising of US$5.8m, explains Co-Founder Tzar Taraporvala
The food industry is a critical part of the global supply chain, but it is also becoming increasingly complex.
With ongoing disruption in the form of climate change impacting crop production, food supply chains are undergoing a period of vulnerability.
Alongside this, an
ageing workforce
and a growing skills gap is putting pressure elsewhere in the chain.
Anchr, therefore, was founded with the aim of simplifying and modernising the food distribution industry in order to drive
efficiency and resilience
within the sector.
A critical industry
The food distribution industry is one of incredible scale and huge importance. Massive amounts of food are distributed around the world every day, being transported across land, seas and skies to get to its final destination.
With this, however, comes a significant amount of risk. Food waste is a major problem within the industry, as products need to be kept in carefully controlled temperatures to arrive in the ideal condition, and certain products get damaged in transit.
It is a complex supply chain, made up of fast hand-offs, regular temperature checks and a knowledge that speed is key.
However, with increasing regulations, ongoing volatility and worsening climate conditions, the food distribution network is even more complex than it ever has been.
To meet modern expectations and navigate this complexity, Anchr has been developed. This platform is an AI operating system, working to unify sales, operations, logistics, inventory and finance into a single layer. Fragmented ERP data becomes transformed into actionable insights and
real-time visibility
Through this, teams can reduce waste, protect margin and execute actions faster.
The numbers
With anchr, users are seeing 99% less errors and less operational waste
Businesses are witnessing healthier finances with 30% more margin
15k+ hours have been saved
Anchr raised US$5.8m
With the Order Intake Agent, there is a projected US$350k in annual productivity gain
Tzar Taraporvala and Smayan Mehra Co-Founders at Anchr
Modernising workflows
Anchr was co-founded by childhood best friends Smayan Mehra and Tzar Taraporvala. With an aim of tackling some of the most impactful challenges in the industry, the pair set out to build the first end-to-end AI operating system.
Food distributors source, move and deliver the vast majority of the food we eat. They are the operational backbone of the
food supply chain
. And yet, this trillion-dollar industry still runs on fragmented software, manual workflows and systems built decades ago. The result is labor shortages, margin compression and massive operational inefficiency across a sector that the country depends on every single day.
Tzar Taraporvala, Co-Founder at Anchr, on LinkedIn
Earlier this year, the AI-powered
startup raised
US$5.8m in order to modernise the back-office functions of the food distribution network. Its investors included Anterra Capital, a16z Speedrun and Offline Ventures.
Anchr’s agents are directly embedded into a distributor’s workflows, automating administration and providing customers with increased operating leverage.
Food supply chains are becoming increasingly complex. Credit: Unsplash
Industry-wide solutions
Though it started as a food company, its solutions are being used across a range of industries, working across businesses that buy and move physical products.
Its solutions are being used across Industrial & MRO, moving parts, tools and maintenance supplies that are critical for operations.
Anchr is also being used in the healthcare and pharmaceutical industry, as the products need to meet heightened regulatory requirements and need thorough
traceability standards
. Anchr’s agents offer these capabilities, with reliable and dependable data.
Items that have specialised and technical needs, such as electrical and plumbing products are also being transported with greater efficiency due to Anchr’s technology.
Around the world, companies are seeing the mass benefits of automating their back-office functions, with cost savings, productivity gains and greater accuracy.
We are building the first end-to-end AI operating system for supply chains, designed to automate the tedious back-office work that has burdened this industry for far too long. We don't just go end-to-end, we provide a truly bespoke solution.
Smayan Mehra, Co-Founder at Anchr

content:
Peter Johnson

The Pixo is back, but this time it’s an all-electric city cruiser set to become
Nissan’s
most affordable EV starting under $25,000.
Meet the Nissan Pixo EV, an affordable electric city car
After discontinuing the budget city car in 2013, Nissan is reviving the Pixo name for its new entry-level EV.
The Pixo EV marks Nissan’s return to Europe’s minicar segment, which is seeing a surge of low-cost electric vehicles primarily driven by Chinese automakers like BYD and Leapmotor.
European legacy automakers, such as Volkswagen and Renault, are leading a counter-offensive, with new EVs like the ID. Polo and the Dacia Spring.
Nissan is the latest with plans to enter Europe’s growing electric A-segment market. Developed through its partnership with Renualt, the Pixo EV shares the same underpinnings as the Renault Twingo.
It uses a 27.5 kWh lithium iron phosphate battery, the first LFP battery in a Nissan EV in Europe, providing a WLTP range of up to 259 km (161 miles).
Using a 50 kW DC fast charger, the Pixo EV’s battery can charge from 15% to 80% in about 28 minutes.
Nissan said the new Pixo EV is designed for “drivers looking for an accessible electric city car that combines compact dimensions, practical interior space, modern connectivity and everyday usability.”
Measuring 3,796 mm long, 1,790 mm wide, and 1,512 mm tall, with a 2,492 mm wheelbase, Nissan’s new Pixo EV is nearly identical in size to the Renault Twingo and Hyundai Inster.
Although it’s an entry-level model, the electric city car will be equipped with advanced driver assistance systems, including automated emergency braking, lane-keeping assist, and e-Pedal technology.
It also has Google built-in, including Gemini, providing “intuitive” navigation, such as real-time route planning and charging, which can be accessed through the MyNissan app.
The Pixo EV is designed by Nissan, but will be produced at Renault’s Novo Mesto manufacturing plant in Slovenia.
“As fuel costs rise, the case for switching to electrified vehicles only grows stronger. Nissan is right at the heart of that shift,” Massimiliano Messina, Chairperson, Nissan AMIEO, said after unveiling the new entry-level EV on Wednesday.

title: Tesla’s 'hardcore lawyers' went a little too hardcore
content:
Tesla’s racism trial in California opened Monday with a bad day for the company’s lawyers. The first witness testified that a senior Tesla in-house attorney had called him last week and let him believe he was working for the state, according to Law360 (paywall).
That same morning, Tesla’s outside counsel told the judge the N-word is a “term of respect and endearment” in the Black community. Both happened in front of Judge Peter Borkon, the one person who will decide the case.
Back in May 2022, three months after California first sued Tesla over racism at Fremont, Elon Musk announced that Tesla was building a “hardcore litigation department where we directly initiate and execute lawsuits,” with the team reporting directly to him. We found the timing strange back then, and Monday gave a good look at what “hardcore” means in practice.
Musk also promised Tesla would never settle an unjust case. It has since settled another racism lawsuit and partly settled the Vaughn class action, with about 580 workers still pressing individual claims.
But Tesla’s ‘hardcore lawyers’ went a little too hardcore in this case. Some would even call it witness tampering.
The call from Tesla’s lawyer
The California Civil Rights Department (CRD) is suing Tesla on behalf of more than 6,000 Black workers at its Fremont factory, as we reported when the trial opened. It’s a bench trial in Alameda County Superior Court, damages are uncapped, and it’s expected to run through October.
The CRD’s first witness was former Tesla worker Ryan Edwards. At the end of his direct examination, he told Borkon about a call last week from Timothy Kim, senior corporate counsel on Tesla’s employment litigation team.
Kim left a voicemail saying he was an attorney “handling the Tesla civil rights case,” Edwards testified. They then talked for about 30 minutes. Over that call, Kim kept steering him toward saying Tesla wasn’t a bad place to work, and even that it was the best job he ever had.
Edwards had his own lawyer at the time. Kim offered to represent him anyway and asked what settlements he’d signed or would consider. Edwards said it was only when Kim started reciting the full names of his old Tesla managers and supervisors that he understood the lawyer was on Tesla’s side, not the state’s.
Kim’s LinkedIn profile carries a single quote from Thomas Jefferson next to his job title: “We prefer war in all cases to tribute under any form and to any people whatever.”
Four more witnesses gone quiet
CRD attorney Juan Gamboa asked Borkon to bar Tesla’s counsel from contacting anyone on the agency’s witness list.
He told the court the CRD had tried to reach at least four other listed witnesses over the past several days without getting a response, and that they’ve fallen “off our radar.” The agency believes Tesla’s lawyers got to them too, either with payments not to testify or by talking them out of it. Gamboa wants to stop Tesla from offering to represent witnesses “through persuasion and payment.”
Borkon didn’t rule on it right away. During a break, he told the CRD to file a formal motion if it wants the order. Tesla hasn’t commented publicly, and it no longer has a PR department to ask.
‘The N-word is not on trial here’
Tesla’s trial lawyer is Tyree P. Jones Jr. of Polsinelli PC. In his opening, he pointed to rap lyrics from Kanye West and Jay-Z to argue the slur is a term of endearment in the Black community. “This trial is not about the N-word — the N-word is not on trial here,” Jones said.
His case is that Tesla has “don’t do stupid stuff” policies, keeps adequate records, disciplines misconduct, and brought 20,000 jobs to Fremont. “The question is what is there to enjoin? The answer to that is: nothing,” he said.
The testimony that followed didn’t help. Edwards said a non-Black coworker called him the N-word, cursed at him, and threatened to beat him up. He reported it right away. A month later, he found out his managers had written him up over the incident, and he was later passed over for promotions after applying to more than 100 jobs.
The CRD’s Brett Watson told the court the evidence will show managers calling Tesla “the plantation,” with some referring to themselves and Elon Musk as “slave masters,” and graffiti including swastikas, “KKK,” and nooses left on factory walls for days.
The second witness, former regional security manager Ozell Murray, testified that his supervisor, Ray Sethna, now Tesla’s senior director of global security, told him to warn a Black Marine veteran he was hiring: “just be sure [the veteran] knows he’ll be called those words.”
Electrek’s Take
Lawyers talk to former employees before trial all the time. But California’s professional conduct rules are clear on two things: you don’t contact someone about a case when you know they have a lawyer, and you don’t let an unrepresented person misunderstand whose side you’re on. Edwards had a lawyer, and by his account, he spent a good part of a 30-minute call thinking Tesla’s attorney worked for the state.
Then 4 other witnesses contacted the same way have disappeared from the case.
Top comment by Beario
Building a hardcore legal team is something you do when you know you have problems and you want to minimize the damage that is coming. It is highly unlikely that 6000 people would have so many stories to tell about an abusive work environment that clearly wasn't managing the conditions correctly and anyone filing complaints were exposed to retaliation. It will be interesting to see the extent things went as the facts unfold in these cases.
Tesla will get to tell its side. But look at what the call was for, according to the testimony. Get a Black former worker, in a case about Black workers being called “slaves,” to say Tesla was the best job he ever had. Ask what settlement he’d take. Offer to be his lawyer. That’s not a witness interview.
And then there’s the defense strategy. Arguing that the N-word is a term of endearment, in a trial where the first witness says a non-Black coworker used it while threatening to beat him up, is not really endearing. So is doing it in front of the judge who alone decides whether Tesla gets hit with an injunction and uncapped damages.
Musk wanted a hardcore litigation team, and one of its lawyers apparently has a Jefferson quote about preferring war on his LinkedIn. Mission accomplished. We’ll see if Borkon is impressed.
Whatever happens in that courtroom, the cheapest way to power any EV is still with your own rooftop solar. title: Donut Lab really wants us to believe its 'miracle solid-state battery' is real
content:
Donut Lab
Fred Lambert
| Sep 23 2026 - 6:27 am PT
An Intertek lab in the UK found just 3.4 ppm of lithium in a sample of Donut Lab’s “solid-state” battery, and the Finnish startup is now using that result to argue its cell is neither lithium-ion nor sodium-ion.
But the report measured just two elements, on a cell Donut Lab took apart itself. And nine months after CES, there’s still no production vehicle running on the battery.
A two-element test
The Finnish startup says the goal was to end the debate over what’s inside its cell. “We wanted to put this speculation to rest with an independent test demonstrating that it is neither a lithium-ion nor a sodium battery,” CEO Marko Lehtimäki said in the announcement.
That speculation didn’t come out of nowhere. In June, battery researcher Ziroth and more than 20 experts
concluded that the cell Donut Lab sent to VTT behaved like a high-nickel lithium-ion cell with a graphite anode
, based on its voltage curve and swelling data.
Intertek’s report
, from its lab in Wilton, UK, is short. Analysts cut about 0.5 g of material from anode, cathode, and current collector pieces, digested it in nitric acid, diluted it to 50 ml, and ran it through an ICP-OES instrument. Results: 3.4 ppm lithium and 632 ppm sodium by weight.
A lithium-ion cell carries lithium in the percent range. So if that sample is what Donut Lab says it is, there’s essentially no lithium in it.
The lab work itself is fine. The problems start with everything around it.
What the report doesn’t show
Start with the scope. The job Donut Lab ordered was literally “Quantification of Li and Na by ICP-OES.” Nothing else was measured. The report tells you two things the cell isn’t and zero things about what it is. Potassium, magnesium, zinc, and aluminum were never tested, and Donut Lab still won’t name its chemistry beyond “widely available, affordable and geopolitically secure materials.”
Then there’s the sample. According to Intertek, “the samples were delivered in a tear down condition by Donut Lab.” Intertek didn’t open a cell. It matched the pieces to another Intertek report (2608094STO-003) that hasn’t been made public, and the analyzed sample is labeled simply “Pouchcell – Cell 1.” The words “Donut Battery” appear nowhere in the report, and nothing ties this sample to the V1.5 cell that VTT tested for energy density.
The press release also says the samples included “the electrolyte situated between” the anode and cathode. Intertek’s report says otherwise, three separate times: only anode, cathode, and current collector parts were analyzed. In a solid-state battery, the electrolyte layer is a pretty important place to look for lithium.
And the report went through three versions in five days. The first was issued September 17. A September 21 revision updated the “sample description and origin of samples,” and a September 22 revision made a “wording change requested in experimental.” That’s a lot of editing for a report with a single two-column results table.
Finally, Intertek notes that “opinions and interpretations contained herein are outside the scope of UKAS accreditation.” The line that “it is not even possible to build a functional battery with such small amounts of active materials” comes from Donut CTO Ville Piippo, not the lab.
It makes the 409 Wh/kg claim harder to believe
Near-zero lithium and sodium fits one theory that has followed Donut Lab since CES: a supercapacitor or hybrid capacitor, with carbon electrodes and an electrolyte that doesn’t rely on either element. That would line up with the fast-charging and cycle-life claims. It wouldn’t line up with energy density.
Earlier this month, VTT measured
409.3 Wh/kg on a Donut “V1.5” cell
, cycled between 2.3 V and 4.25 V. That’s a textbook lithium-ion voltage window, and 409 Wh/kg is a number advanced silicon-anode lithium-ion cells already hit.
No rechargeable chemistry without lithium or sodium has come anywhere close to that in a real cell. So either Donut Lab has quietly invented a chemistry that beats every battery lab on the planet, or the cell VTT tested and the pieces Intertek analyzed aren’t the same thing. This report doesn’t tell us which.
Electrek’s Take
We don’t care much anymore whether Donut Lab’s battery is solid-state and these vague and limited tests that may or may not prove otherwise do very little to Donut Lab’s credibility.
Solid-state cells exist. QuantumScape, Factorial, Samsung SDI, and Toyota all have them running in labs and prototype vehicles, and all of them are still working toward mass production. A startup with a promising solid-state prototype is not news in 2026.
The only thing that made Donut Lab interesting was the production claim. At CES in January, it said it had the “world’s first solid state battery that is ready for use in OEM vehicle manufacturing,” with
Verge motorcycles delivering to customers in Q1 2026
. Lehtimäki said it was “already in production.”
We’re now at the end of September. There’s no production vehicle on the road with this battery, the Q1 “production” bikes were pre-production units, and Lehtimäki himself admitted that the 409 Wh/kg cell “is not even the cell that’s going to be shipped to customers.”
So the claim that set Donut apart turned out to be wrong, and every new report since has been built to answer a different question than the one that matters.

title: Get paid to charge, a free charger, *and* save the grid with a new GM EV in CA
content:
GM Energy
Jameson Dow
| Sep 23 2026 - 6:00 am PT
General Motors and Pacific Gas and Electric are running a deal to give new EV buyers a free charger, get paid to charge, and save the grid all at the same time. What’s not to love?
Much has been said about the strain on the grid that could be produced by EVs. If we suddenly put all the energy use that cars represent onto a grid that’s already overloaded, won’t that be an issue?
In a naive view perhaps… but in fact, electric cars can
the grid
Currently, electric grids fluctuate throughout the day, usually somewhat predictably. People use more electricity when it’s hot or cold out (to run HVAC), and more electricity in the evening hours when doing chores like cooking and laundry. And typically people use the least electricity at night, when they’re asleep.
But it’s harder to run power plants for just a couple hours every day, which means electricity is expensive in those hours of peaks in demand, and cheaper in the troughs in demand.
The beauty of electric cars, though, is that they have large batteries and therefore can be charged at whenever is the most opportune time throughout the day. This is usually nighttime, but not always (for example, in Australia, they have so much solar they’re
literally giving it away
during the day).
This is why utilities often offer “time of use” rates, giving cheaper electricity at off-peak times. Many EV drivers have taken advantage of this to charge up for cheap, making driving an EV even more comparatively cheap at a time when
unnecessary conflict drives gas prices higher everywhere
But sometimes time of use rates aren’t enough, so another concept has come forward: managed charging.
Remote-controlled charging can save the grid and make you money
This utilizes a constant internet connection, either from the charger or the EV charging on it, so let a utility remotely control your charge sessions, charging when there is an excess of electricity on the grid. In practice, you tell the system how full you want your car to be and when, and then the system handles the rest.
In return, utilities offer some sort of incentive. It saves them money to do this, so they pass the savings on to you. This is usually in the form of a credit on your electricity bill.
PG&E, in Northern and Central California, has a program for this which it calls its
“Charge Manager” program
. Other utilities have a similar program, like
SoCal Edison’s Charge Ready program
. They usually require a specific type of charger or car that supports the protocols used to manage your charging sessions.
These programs differ from “bidirectional charging” or V2G/V2H programs you might have heard of, as they don’t actually require you to send any energy back to the grid, merely to wait to charge until the times that the grid wants you to charge. So it’s a lot easier in terms of installing equipment, as you really just need a charger that can be controlled remotely.
And now, PG&E and GM Energy are pairing up to offer an incentive on new GM EVs that helps get them on a managed charging program like this
GM and PG&E’s new deal pays you for helping with grid resilience
new program announced today
, which GM is calling the “Smart Charge Bundle,” offers a free GM PowerShift ($1,399-$1,999) or PowerUp2 ($899) home charger when a new GM EV is purchased from a participating GM dealer in Northern or Central California by a buyer who has PG&E residential service. You’ll have to pay for installation, and use GM’s selected installation partner (Electrum) to install the equipment.
Then, once you have the participating charger, as long as you have OnStar (GM’s connected vehicle software), you’ll get a $15 monthly bill credit for participation in the Charge Manager program, and an additional up to $50 per month based on how much of your charging gets shifted onto optimal times.
The deal covers basically all of GM’s electric model line – any Chevrolet, Cadillac or GMC EV, and will run until February 2027 or until the program hits its capacity.
If you’re looking for a GM EV and live in PG&E’s service area, you can use our links below to reach out to local dealers about these popular EVs. But definitely ask if they’re participating in the Smart Charge Bundle program before you go all in:
2027 Chevy Bolt EV
2027 Chevy Equinox EV
2027 Chevy Blazer EV
2027 Chevy SIlverado EV
2027 GMC Sierra EV
2027 Cadillac Optiq
2027 Cadillac Lyriq
2027 Cadillac Vistiq
2027 Cadillac Escalade IQ
Then, you can head over to
PG&E’s enrollment portal for GM Energy products
to make sure you’re all signed up.

title: Trucks gone wild! VinFast launches VF Wild EREV pickup
content:
electric trucks
Jo Borrás
| Sep 23 2026 - 5:25 am PT
With more than 250 km (~155 miles) of battery-only range, genuine off-road capability, and a range extending ICE motor that pushes total range well past 1,000 km (~620 miles), VinFast’s new VF Wild is shaping up to be an interesting entry in the electrified truck race.
First shown as an all-electric concept back in 2024
, the production version of the new VF Wild pickup is still motivated by an electric motor putting out 160 kW (~215 hp) and 280 Nm (~205 lb-ft.) of torque drawing power from a relatively modest 46.4 kWh LFP battery pack (
compared to the monster 205 kWh battery in GM’s electric trucks
, anyway). That setup is good enough to get VF Wild drivers about 250 km away (NEDC) from where they started before the ICE generator kicks in to keep the party going.
But, crucially,
that’s all it does
. VinFast is quick to point out that its internal combustion engine is purely a range-extender, and that the vehicle is driven solely by its electric motors for a driving experience that’s much closer to a “pure” EV than it is to a conventional hybrid.
Information on the ICE is limited, but Vietnamese-language
is reporting a 1.5L petrol (gas)
engine under the hood
Shooting for the stars
VF Wild, after dark; by VinFast.
The cold, hard numbers on this thing are interesting. At 5,376 mm long, 2,069 mm wide, and 1,873 mm tall with a 3,258-mm wheelbase, the VF Wild seems to be taking aim at industry heavyweights like the Ford Ranger and
Toyota HiLux
, but those can’t be had as EREV’s, making me think of the old adage that goes “aim for the moon, end up among the stars.”
It remains to be seen how well the new VF Wild will do in the global market, but it seems worth noting that VinGroup (VIC.VN)
is profitable
. The company had a record 2025 posting more than $12.8 billion in revenue and nearly $430 million in net (not gross)
unlike some pretty notable others in the industry
they’re currently expanding their global operations
No word yet on any plans to bring the VF Wild to North America – if and when it ever does arrive, however, it will probably be priced right. The starting price for the new VinFast EREV pickup is “just” 860 million
, which works out to ~33,000USD as I type this.
Inside, the truck features a flat floor, a 10″ touchscreen infotainment system in the center console spot, and reclining rear seats. Like other VinFast models (and the Saturn Ion, and first-gen Toyota Prius), the VF Wild lacks an instrument cluster in front of the driver. title: Poland offers 76 TWh in November renewables auctions - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Poland’s Energy Regulatory Office (URE) has put almost PLN 25 billion ($6.5 billion) of renewables support up for bid in November, with PV and onshore wind taking most of it.
Brian Publicover
23 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Katowice, Poland
Poland’s Energy Regulatory Office (URE) will run seven price-only auctions for new renewable energy installations from Nov. 2 to Nov. 10, with PV and onshore wind allocated most of the support on offer.
The auctions can award support for a little more than 76 TWh of renewable electricity worth almost PLN 25 billion, URE said on Sept. 22. Of that total, 64.5 TWh worth a little more than PLN 17.9 billion is reserved for PV and onshore wind.
The largest pot, 53.25 TWh, is set aside for PV and onshore wind projects larger than 1 MW, which will compete in the final auction, AZ/7/2026, on Nov. 10.
Bids will be assessed on price alone, and only new installations can take part, under a 2022 government regulation that sets maximum auction volumes and values for each year through 2027. Maximum bid prices are set by a November 2023 regulation from the Ministry of Climate and Environment.
In last year’s equivalent auction, AZ/7/2025, held July 9, 2025, URE received 98 bids and selected 76, at prices ranging from PLN 100.00/MWh to PLN 329.68/MWh, according to results the regulator published July 11, 2025. Of the 129 winning bids across the 2025 round, 126 were for PV projects and three for onshore wind,
with PV allocations totaling 1.67 GW
URE said auctions held since 2016 have contracted nearly 307 TWh of renewable electricity, worth close to PLN 77 billion.

title: Amazon, Nadara switch on 277 MW agrivoltaic facility in Italy - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Nadara has completed the 227 MW Big Fish agrivoltaic project in Sicily, backed by a 156 MW PPA with Amazon and described by the developer as Italy’s largest agrivoltaic facility. The 400-hectare project was approved with a 20 MW/40 MWh battery energy storage system.
Massimiliano Tripodo
23 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
UK-based renewable energy company Nadara has completed a 227 MW agrivoltaic project in Sicily that it describes as the largest facility of its kind in Italy.
The Big Fish project is located in the province of Catania. According to Nadara, construction was supported by a previously signed 156 MW power purchase agreement (PPA) with Amazon.
Located around 40 km from Mount Etna, the project extends across the municipalities of Catania, Lentini and Motta Sant’Anastasia. Nadara said the facility was built in 12 months, with more than 900 workers involved in construction.
The project covers around 400 hectares across 15 plots, with approximately half of the area dedicated to agricultural activities.
Nadara estimates that local municipalities will receive at least €17.25 million for services and energy-efficiency measures over the project’s operating life. The funding will support infrastructure upgrades, monitoring systems for public buildings and electric vehicles for municipal use.
The developer said environmental mitigation measures included the planting of 38,000 trees and maintenance work along 2.5 km of public waterways.
To accommodate agricultural activities, the solar panels were installed at heights of up to 3 meters. Overhead cables were routed around the perimeter of the site, while 14 wells were built or restored to provide irrigation. Beehives installed at the project are expected to produce around 4.5 metric tons of honey per year.
Regional documents show that the project’s environmental approval included a 20 MW/40 MWh battery energy storage system. Environmental approval was granted in May 2023, followed by final permit in October 2023. Subsequent approvals explicitly identify Big Fish as an agrivoltaic project including cover retention basins, hydraulic crossings and other works. In September 2025, regional authorities certified compliance with the environmental conditions imposed under the 2023 approval.
Amazon, which has set a target of reaching net-zero carbon emissions across its operations by 2040, said it has supported eight utility-scale solar projects in Italy and installed 32 solar systems at its facilities in the country. The 40 projects have a combined estimated capacity of 532 MW.
At 227 MW, Big Fish is slightly larger than European Energy’s 225.5 MW agrivoltaic project in Vizzini, also in the province of Catania, where construction began in May.

title: Blue wafers are fundamentally undermining U.S. solar manufacturing - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The core debate shaping U.S. solar manufacturing isn’t just factory capacity, but whether facilities perform the critical P/N junction process on raw “gray” wafers or merely finish partially completed “blue” wafers imported from abroad.
Sekhar Tatineni
23 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Manufacturing
As the United States builds a more resilient solar supply chain, the industry’s attention and data collection has primarily focused on factory capacity: how many gigawatts have been announced, how quickly facilities can begin production and where new manufacturing operations are located.
There is an often overlooked aspect of this process, however: What material enters the factory before the cells are produced? The answer can reveal whether a facility is performing the core processes, specifically P/N Junction, required to manufacture a solar cell or completing a limited number of steps on a product that has already undergone its most important transformation overseas.
This distinction is at the center of the growing discussion surrounding “gray wafers” and “blue wafers.” While the terms may sound highly esoteric, the issue has significant implications for domestic manufacturing policy, tax-credit eligibility, trade compliance and the credibility of the U.S. solar supply chain.
When does a wafer become a cell?
A gray wafer is an unprocessed silicon wafer, meaning it cannot generate electricity on its own. Turning it into a functioning solar cell requires a series of highly controlled manufacturing processes that alter its surface, electrical properties and performance.
Although specific production sequences vary by cell architecture, these processes typically include texturing and cleaning the wafer, junction formation, edge isolation, passivation, anti-reflective coating application, metallization and testing.
Among these steps, formation of the photovoltaic junction is particularly significant. The starting crystalline-silicon wafer may be either p-type or n-type. During cell manufacturing, a layer of the opposite conductivity type is introduced to form the junction necessary for photovoltaic operation. Depending on the cell architecture, this may be achieved through high-temperature dopant diffusion or through deposition of doped semiconductor layers. The junction creates the electric field that allows the device to separate charge carriers and convert sunlight into electricity. It is one of the defining technical transformations in solar cell manufacturing.
A blue wafer has its P/N junction already formed by the time it reaches the factory, and it has typically received the anti-reflective coating that gives it its blue appearance. While metallization and other finishing processes may still be required, the wafer already has the fundamental semiconductor structure that enables photovoltaic conversion.
This is why describing both materials simply as “wafers” can obscure an important difference. A gray wafer is a raw input to solar-cell manufacturing. A blue wafer is much closer to a partially completed solar cell.
Why process location matters
The current debate is about identifying where substantive manufacturing occurred.
A facility that imports gray wafers and performs the critical cell-making processes domestically is carrying out a different scope of manufacturing than a facility that imports blue wafers and completes only the remaining downstream steps.
Both operations may require equipment, workers and quality controls. However, they do not necessarily represent the same level of technical transformation, manufacturing value or domestic capability.
Policymakers have started evaluating whether federal incentives are supporting the development of an enduring U.S. solar manufacturing base. Incentives designed to encourage domestic solar cell production are most effective when they support the processes, equipment, engineering expertise and workforce required to transform a gray wafer into a functioning cell.
If nearly completed cells can enter the country as wafers and receive the same treatment as cells manufactured domestically from their initial stage, the market may reward finishing operations the same way it rewards more comprehensive manufacturing. Over time, that could weaken the incentive to invest in the full range of capabilities the United States offers.
Different rules may produce different answers
One reason the issue is complex is that “domestic” can mean different things under different regulatory frameworks.
Tax incentives, customs classifications, domestic content requirements, and antidumping and countervailing duty rules are governed by different statutes and administrative standards. A product’s treatment under one framework does not automatically determine its treatment under another.
For example, domestic content calculations examine where specific manufactured products and components are produced and how their costs are accounted for. Customs and trade authorities may apply separate standards when determining a product’s country of origin or whether duties apply.
In solar trade proceedings, the location where the P/N junction is formed has historically been an important factor in determining a solar cell’s origin. That reflects the technical significance of junction formation in creating a device capable of photovoltaic conversion.
The industry should therefore be careful not to rely on a single broad claim, such as “U.S.-made,” as a substitute for a process-specific compliance analysis. The relevant question is which manufacturing steps occurred in each country and how those steps are treated under the particular rule being applied.
Why this matters beyond the manufacturer
Questions about wafer processing can create risk throughout the solar value chain.
Module manufacturers rely on cell suppliers’ representations to determine product origin and calculate domestic content levels. Developers may use that information to model project economics and support eligibility for federal incentives. Tax-credit investors, lenders and insurers may evaluate the same documentation as part of project diligence.
If the underlying manufacturing process has been inaccurately described, the consequences may extend beyond the original supplier. Domestic content calculations could be challenged, expected incentives could be reduced and contracts could become the subject of disputes over pricing, indemnification or responsibility for inaccurate representations.
This does not mean every product involving imported blue wafers is necessarily noncompliant. The treatment will depend on the applicable law, the specific production process and the facts surrounding the transaction. It does mean that buyers and other stakeholders should understand precisely what they are purchasing and avoid treating all U.S.-
finished
cells as technically or legally equivalent.
Documentation must follow the manufacturing process
As the market matures, traceability will become as important as production capacity. A credible chain of documentation should identify the material entering the U.S. facility, where the P/N junction was formed, and which manufacturing processes were performed domestically. It should also connect those records to the finished cells and modules being supplied.
Useful diligence questions include:
What condition is the wafer in when it enters the United States?
Where does P/N junction formation occur?
Which passivation, coating and metallization processes are performed domestically?
How is the imported material classified?
Can production records trace finished cells back to specific incoming materials and process steps?
Are tax, customs and trade representations supported independently?
How are compliance responsibilities allocated in customer contracts?
These questions should become part of routine procurement rather than an exceptional audit exercise. Clear documentation protects responsible manufacturers while giving customers greater confidence in their sourcing and incentive calculations.
The industry needs process-based definitions
The blue wafer debate highlights a broader challenge for U.S. clean energy policy: Manufacturing cannot be measured solely by a factory’s address or the location of its final production step.
Effective policy must recognize where meaningful technical transformations occur. For solar cells, that requires examining the manufacturing sequence and determining where a silicon wafer acquires the characteristics that make it a photovoltaic device.
Clear, consistently applied definitions would benefit the entire market. Manufacturers would have greater certainty when making capital investments. Buyers would be better able to compare suppliers. Developers and investors could make more defensible incentive claims. Policymakers could more accurately evaluate whether public support is producing the domestic capabilities it was intended to create.
The U.S. has an opportunity to build a solar manufacturing base grounded in technical depth, operational transparency and long-term credibility. Achieving that goal requires the industry to look beyond where a product is finished and ask a more fundamental question: Where did the wafer actually become a solar cell?

title: Ukraine adds 1.1 GW of solar in H1 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Analysis from the Solar Energy Association of Ukraine estimates the country’s solar capacity reached up to 9.7 GW by mid-2026.
Patrick Jowett
23 Sep 2026

Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Highlights
