title: Stillstrom partners with Semco Maritime on offshore charging technology
content:
Stillstrom and Semco Maritime have signed a letter of intent (LOI) to manufacture
and deliver elements of a new offshore power and charging solution.
The Local Equipment Room (LER) controls power, communication and safety
systems across the charging infrastructure. It houses the transformer,
medium-voltage switchgear, communication equipment, ventilation systems
and fire safety equipment.
"The LER is extremely significant to our solution, as it acts as the
nerve centre of our charging system. It controls everything that happens,
with one another," said Gordon Dickson, operations and maintenance
lead at Stillstrom UK.
The agreement follows the completion of the LER design phase, which was
carried out by Semco Maritime.
Stephen Booth, vice president of renewable service at Semco Maritime, said:
"This milestone reflects the strong collaboration we've built with
Stillstrom through the design phase, and we're proud to carry that into
manufacturing at our Esbjerg facility."
As part of a separate LOI between Semco Maritime and Siemens, Siemens will
supply the switchgear and control systems.

title: New York leads lawsuits over cancelled offshore wind leases
content:
New York Attorney General Letitia James and Governor Kathy Hochul have
announced two lawsuits challenging agreements between the Trump administration
and developers Bluepoint Wind and Invenergy.
The states argue the agreements unlawfully cancelled four offshore wind
projects and redirected federal funds to other energy developments.
Under the agreements, Bluepoint Wind received $765 million and Invenergy
received $653 million from the federal Judgment Fund. The developers agreed
to cancel offshore wind leases, including projects located off the coast
of New York.
According to the announcement the cancelled New York offshore wind projects
were expected to attract more than $16 billion in investment and create

title: OSRL launches new shallow-water deployment capability
content:
OSRL has announced the launch of a new shallow-water deployment capability.
The innovation aims to strengthen source control preparedness for difficult
well control scenarios.
The company has integrated two systems: OSRL's Split Lowering System (SLS),
developed in partnership with InterMoor, and the Snub Line Winch System,
developed by Oceaneering.
When combined, these systems enable capping stack deployment when conditions
make vertical access unsafe.
Vania De Stefani, chief executive officer at OSRL, said: "This shallow-water
deployment capability reflects OSRL's continued investment in strengthening
industry readiness for complex subsea incidents."
Adding: "By bringing together the Split Lowering System and Snub Line
Winch System, it helps support safer, controlled capping stack deployment
in challenging shallow-water scenarios and reinforces the value of collaborative
preparedness across the industry."
The benefits of this new technology include improved control during the
final landing sequence, supported deployment in water depths ranging from
75 to 600 metres, rapid mobilisation from OSRL's Norway base, and installation
without seabed interface components.

title: Inch Cape completes second offshore export cable installation
content:
Inch Cape Offshore Wind Farm
has officially completed installation of the second of two 220 kV three
phase offshore export cables.
The 85 kilometre cable was installed in three 28 kilometre sections by
Enshore Subsea using the cable lay vessel CMOS Installer.
The installation programme included two offshore joints completed aboard
Normand Cutter. The cable was buried using the ENS1100 hybrid trenching
vehicle, with final rock placement still to be completed.
The two parallel export cables will connect the project's offshore substation
platform to a new onshore substation at Cockenzie, East Lothian, before
linking to the national grid.
The 2,000mm² export cable was manufactured by Orient Cable and weighs almost
140 tonnes per kilometre. A total of 170 kilometres of export cable has
been installed for the 1.1 GW wind farm.
John Hill, Inch Cape Project Director said: “The completion of this crucial
link between the offshore and onshore substations is another major achievement
for the project and testament to the excellent collaboration between the
Inch Cape team and our contractors, particularly Orient Cable and Enshore
Subsea.”

title: Borkum Riffgrund 3 has been officially inaugurated
content:
The 913 MW
Borkum Riffgrund 3 offshore
wind farm has been officially inaugurated, according to project partners
Ørsted and Nuveen.
The project is expected to be Germany's
largest offshore wind farm and will generate enough renewable electricity
to power nearly 1 million German households.
Rasmus Errboe, CEO of Ørsted, said: "Borkum Riffgrund 3 shows what

The announcement emphasises the offshore wind farm's contribution to Germany's
renewable energy targets, supporting the country's energy security and
competitiveness. This is particularly significant as Germany still imports
60% of its energy, leaving households and businesses vulnerable to increases
in fossil fuel prices.
Katherina Reiche, Germany's federal minister for economic affairs and energy,
said: "This single project adds nearly a tenth to our national offshore
capacity, which has already surpassed 10 GW this year."
The project was constructed using the European offshore wind supply chain,
including wind turbines and foundations from Germany and Denmark, cables
and Belgium.

title: DeepOcean and TFKable Group to develop integrated inter-array cable offering
content:
DeepOcean and TFKable Group to develop integrated inter-array cable offering TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
DeepOcean and TFKable Group to develop integrated inter-array cable offering
DeepOcean and TFKable Group have entered a joint venture focused on integrated
engineering, procurement, construction and installation services for inter-array
cable projects, according to the companies announcement.
The collaboration will combine TFKable Group's subsea technology and manufacturing
capabilities with DeepOcean's offshore engineering, installation and seabed
intervention expertise. As part of the agreement, a new inter-array cable-laying
vessel will also be built.
"By combining complementary cable manufacturing and offshore installation
capabilities, we intend to create a more efficient delivery model that
reduces interfaces, strengthens risk management and supports greater project
certainty," said Øyvind Mikaelsen, CEO of DeepOcean.
Drawing on the combined experience of both companies, the partnership will
provide an integrated offering that covers seabed mapping, route surveys,
engineering, cable manufacturing, transportation, installation and cable
protection.
The venture initially plans to focus on inter-array systems, although supporting
other subsea cable projects in the future has not been ruled out.
"TFKable and JDR Cable Systems have developed strong expertise in
inter-array cable solutions, supported by continued investment in technology,
manufacturing capacity and product development," said Piotr Mirek,
a member of the management board of Tele-Fonika Kable and executive director
for supply chains and investments at JDR Cable Systems.
The venture's capabilities are expected to be introduced gradually, with
further development planned through 2029.

title: What To Expect at AI Agenda Live; Crusoe and Thinking Machines Labs Strike a Compute Deal
content: Happy AI Agenda Live day! For those joining us today at SFMOMA , I’m so excited to meet you all and talk about this exciting, if slightly contentious, moment in the AI industry. Our staff and attendees will ask top researchers, founders and executives from OpenAI , Google DeepMind and Nvidia some burning questions. Here are three at the top of my mind. 1. Is consumer AI dead? This year, it seems like every AI company has doubled down on building AI for businesses, leaving consumer AI in the rearview mirror. Part of that is because of the so-called capability overhang , or the gap between consumers’ relatively dim awareness of what AI can do and the tasks AI can actually automate for them. The labs have been adding features in their consumer AI products to provide suggestions to users so they can bridge that gap, but it has yet to be seen how big of an impact that will have. I’m curious if the hype around products like Instinct and Meta’s Muse will revive the frontier labs’ interest in developing AI for consumers. 2. What happened to the AI research overhaul? At the beginning of the year, every researcher was talking about how the AI industry needed a complete overhaul , and how merely scaling up today’s large language models wouldn’t get us to superintelligence. There’s been a massive vibe shift since then, and now researchers are worried that we’re going to get to superintelligence too quickly and AI safety research won’t be able to keep up. What changed, and what’s going to happen to the spat of neolabs that emerged to try and overtake OpenAI and Anthropic by exploiting overlooked research approaches? 3. How are AI application startups and enterprises maintaining their competitive edge as Anthropic and OpenAI go after their businesses? The frontier AI developers are seemingly moving into every industry and application, from financial services to healthcare to law, and are increasingly positioning themselves as the control plane for all work. How are their customers making sure they don’t get subsumed in the process? For some customers, that might mean building their own models or using open-source AI to ensure they don’t become too dependent on the labs. For others, that might mean a hard decision between making their data and features available to outside AI chatbot users or taking a walled garden approach. Here’s what else is going on… Crusoe Signs $65 Million Deal To Help Run Thinking Machines Lab’s Models For Them Fresh off a $3.9 billion funding round, data center firm Crusoe —best known as the developer of OpenAI’s Stargate project—is continuing to diversify beyond the massive AI data centers that put it on the map. The latest: Crusoe is expanding its offering to also run the AI models its customers use for them (called “managed inference”), and announced a $65 million annual contract with Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab on Wednesday. The workload will run on Nvidia’s B200 server chips in part inside Crusoe’s tiny, one-megawatt Spark data centers, said Crusoe’s senior vice president of product management Erwan Menard . Those chips will primarily run (rather than train) AI models, he said. “ We save them time and extend their own engineering capabilities, and they see great value,” said Menard. Crusoe’s engineers will use software to help Thinking Machines run models more efficiently. Crusoe announced a similar arrangement with Perplexity earlier this month. Crusoe’s managed inference product launched last November and has contracted more than $100 million in annualized recurring revenue, or monthly revenue multiplied by 12, the company has said. Crusoe’s bet on managed inference is part of a broader trend towards companies that help customers run various AI models better and faster, rather than simply serving them raw (or “bare metal”) compute capacity. Together , Fireworks and Baseten are also companies in this category, which has Nvidia’s blessing. Nvidia is an investor in all four, and wants a universe of thousands of personalized AI models running on personalized clouds. Big Number Anthropic is in early talks to lease up to 1 gigawatt in compute capacity from Stream Data Centers , a developer majority-owned by Apollo Global Management , which could house tensor processing units designed by Broadcom and Google , The Information reported Tuesday. Overheard Microsoft leaders told sales staff this week that it is authorizing steeper discounts of 30% to 50% on subscriptions of its Copilot AI software for corporate customers who commit to purchase a large number of seats and commit to additional payments based on their usage of certain features, The Information reported. Meta’ s new personal AI agent, Muse , had more than 500,000 people try it out roughly a week after launch, including more than 250,000 daily active users, according to internal data viewed by The Information. Users have also submitted more than 2 million prompts. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. CoreWeave said on Tuesday it had completed a $4.2 billion convertible bond offering, an upsized amount versus what the AI cloud provider initially targeted last week. Mirendil , an AI startup founded by former Anthropic researchers to build models that can improve themselves with little human help, is in talks to raise up to $1 billion at a $5 billion valuation, including the new investment, in a funding round Kleiner Perkins is in talks to lead, with Andreessen Horowitz also in discussions to invest, Bloomberg reported. Ligent Technologies , a Qingdao AI infrastructure company that makes the optical transceivers and chips data centers use to network their servers together, rose as much as 19.2% in its Hong Kong stock market debut before closing up 4.6%, after raising HK5.7 billion ($727 million) in its initial public offering. Cyera , an AI cybersecurity company, raised $400 million from Goldman Sachs as an extension of the Series G funding round that closed in June, pushing its valuation to over $12 billion. Snorkel AI , which sells the labeled and human-graded data that AI labs need to train their models, raised $350 million in a Series E funding round led by Insight and S32 at a $3.5 billion valuation. Heidi , an Australian startup whose AI drafts doctors’ clinical notes and paperwork for them, raised $340 million to expand its features and its business in Asia and the Middle East. The sum includes a $100 million equity round led by existing investor Blackbird Ventures , which values the company at $900 million. Verda , a Finnish company that rents out AI computing power to compete with the big cloud providers, raised $189 million in a funding round led by Emergence Capital at a valuation the company says is “at least $1 billion.” Micro1 , a San Francisco company that sells the training data AI labs use to teach their models, has raised more than $100 million at a $4 billion valuation, up from about $500 million a year ago, Forbes reported. Go.AI , a Chicago company that sells banks and other regulated businesses AI hardware and software they can run entirely inside their own walls, raised $85 million in a Series A funding round led by Updata Partners . Firecrawl , which builds web-scraping tools that let AI agents pull data from websites, raised $75 million in a Series B funding round led by Smash Ventures . Confido , a New York company whose AI ties together the finance, sales and forecasting data that consumer brands need to manage their retail business, raised $55 million in a Series B funding round led by Insight Partners . Baselayer , a San Francisco company that helps banks verify the businesses and AI agents they work with, raised $35 million in a Series A funding round led by M13 . CellPoint , a London company whose AI helps manage airline and hotel payments, raised $34 million from Toscafund . Planted , a California company whose robots build utility-scale solar farms on hilly land that standard equipment can't handle, raised $31.8 million in a funding round co-led by Piva Capital and RA Capital Management Planetary Health . Biolevate , a Paris company whose AI agents turn scientific and regulatory paperwork into auditable workflows for drug and medical-device makers, raised €30 million in a Series A funding round co-led by RAISE France and Orange Ventures . Chamelio , an Israeli company whose AI drafts, reviews and negotiates contracts so corporate lawyers only have to step in on the cases that need judgment, raised $26 million in a Series A funding round led by Entrée Capital . Sela , a San Francisco company whose AI makes the phone calls and answers borrower questions for mortgage lenders, raised $21 million across seed and Series A funding in a round led by Costanoa . Outerlimit , a London company building security software that checks whether an AI agent is actually authorized before it's allowed to take an action, raised $16 million in a seed funding round from AlbionVC , Evolution Equity Partners , Crane Venture Partners and a group of strategic angel investors. Hong Kong-listed shares of Z.ai and MiniMax plunged on Wednesday, after The Information reported that China’s internet regulator is probing potential data leaks to Anthropic . Z.ai, also known as Zhipu , dropped 12.4%, MiniMax fell 4% and Alibaba declined 4.4%. The benchmark Hang Seng Index dipped 1%. Anthropic announced the release of its newest model , Claude Opus 5.5 , saying it performs as well or better than Anthropic’s previous most powerful models, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 , in domains including coding, reasoning, business workflows, and safety. At the same time, it will cost 40% less to run, according to the announcement on Tuesday. OpenAI on Tuesday announced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna , which it describes as cheaper and faster models in the GPT-6 Astra family. The company said that the new models show significant improvements compared to their predecessors, GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna, in areas like professional work, coding, computer use and accuracy. Anthropic and OpenEvidence , the medical-search platform free to US and European clinicians, are partnering to bring a specialized version of OpenEvidence's AI to physicians in about 100 low- and middle-income countries, including Uganda, Angola, Sudan, Haiti and Mongolia. OpenAI and Grab , a Singapore-based transport and food delivery company, on Wednesday launched a program to train Grab’s drivers, merchants and delivery riders to use ChatGPT for work. Known Systems AI spun out of the domain registrar Identity Digital to build a shared way of holding AI agents accountable to whoever created them — a system called DNSid that its backers describe as a “birth certificate for AI agents,” built on internet domain infrastructure and a blockchain ledger. Identity Digital remains a major investor and keeps a board seat. title: Founders Fund, Khosla Ventures Visit China as Country’s AI Prowess Rises
content: U.S. venture capitalists have slashed investments in Chinese startups in recent years as relations between the two superpowers have soured. But behind the scenes, plenty are taking weekslong trips to meet with the country’s tech founders—a sign of the influence Chinese startups like DeepSeek wield in the hottest parts of tech. Last month, three partners at Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund—Sean Liu, John Luttig and Joey Krug—visited tech companies in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. It was the second trip to China Liu had made in the past year and Luttig’s first visit to the country, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. The idea was not to make investments but to learn about China’s thriving tech sector. Others are taking a similar approach. Khosla Ventures partners have visited tech companies in China two years in a row, according to a person familiar with the visits. Dimension Capital Management, a venture capital firm started by former Lux Capital partners, told its limited partners that the firm spent a week visiting AI labs and entrepreneurs in the country to dig into the competitive edge of China’s startups, as well as the interplay between the country’s AI companies and U.S. ones. David Cheng, a general partner at Costanoa Ventures, said in a post on X earlier this month that he visited China recently to meet with tech companies. Partners from Thrive Capital also visited last year, according to Bloomberg. None of those trips has led to investments in Chinese startups, likely due to U.S. government restrictions and the potential controversies such deals can attract. In addition, some investors say it would be too difficult to monitor the progress of Chinese startups from the U.S. Supply Chain Savvy But the firms still want to learn more about China. The Founders Fund partners went on the recent trip to get a handle on some of their portfolio companies’ dependence on the supply chain in China and how these businesses stack up against Chinese competitors, said one of the people with direct knowledge of the visit. The partners visited advanced manufacturing, robotics, self-driving, energy and AI companies, the person said. Their visit included a trip to the Shanghai headquarters of MiniMax, one of China’s AI model upstarts, according to another person with direct knowledge of the visit, as well as UBTech Robotics in Shenzhen, according to a third person with direct knowledge of the visit. The Khosla partners visited Xiaomi this year and robotics giant Unitree last year. Knowledge of these companies and their hardware suppliers can help investors understand whether a startup in the U.S. is making a product that global competitors are already working on, said the person with knowledge of the visits. Founders Fund’s trip was notable because the firm’s partners have long expressed antipathy toward China. Earlier this year, Thiel claimed that Pope Leo XIV was “working for the Chinese communists” after the Catholic leader called for AI regulation . Partner Trae Stephens criticized American tech companies who backed away from working with the government, saying the lack of public-private partnership in the U.S. has made China “ stronger, richer and more capable .” And partner Delian Asparouhov last year chastised Benchmark for backing the startup behind viral AI agent Manus. (The Chinese government subsequently forced Manus to reverse the $2 billion sale to Meta Platforms reached late last year.) Trips like those of Founders Fund speak to the growing sway of China’s AI industry. In the years since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022, China has gone from an also-ran to a major rival to American frontier labs. That’s largely thanks to the proliferation of startups like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, which are developing open-source models that cost only a fraction of what AI tokens from OpenAI and Anthropic do, and incumbents like ByteDance , whose Seedance ranks high on leaderboards of the best-performing video-generation modes. China has also overtaken U.S. startups when it comes to building humanoid robots; Unitree and AgiBot together shipped 71% of humanoids in the world last year, according to Omdia, and the country controls 63% of the key companies in the global supply chain for humanoid robot components, according to German think tank Mercator Institute for China Studies. China’s supply chain is so essential that employees of some humanoid startups in the U.S. routinely travel to China and fly back home with suitcases stuffed full of prototypes and component samples, The Information reported in August. Many Chinese founders and entrepreneurs are open to meeting with U.S. investors, even if they back rival U.S. startups, in part because they want to stay informed about what’s going on in Silicon Valley, people familiar with these discussions say. Growing Restrictions The Americans’ fact-finding tours are a far cry from the 2000s and 2010s, when U.S. venture capitalists flocked to the country to write checks to startups like TikTok owner ByteDance and ride-hailing provider Didi before they became global powerhouses. But growing worries that China would overtake America’s role as global tech leader has prompted more restrictions. In 2023, President Joe Biden issued an executive order to regulate U.S. investments in China’s semiconductor, AI and quantum computing sectors. That executive order led to official restrictions on outbound investments in Chinese companies in these fields and took effect in early 2025. As Washington increased its scrutiny of U.S. deals in China, American VC funds such as Sequoia Capital and GGV Capital, an early Alibaba investor, separated their America and Asia funds in 2023 and 2024, respectively. So far this year, U.S. VCs participated in 105 deals in China-headquartered companies, nearly flat from 110 deals last year but down 80% from 533 deals in 2021, according to data firm PitchBook. Some Chinese investors have called on U.S. investors to return to the country. Duane Kuang, founding managing partner of Qiming Venture Partners , an early backer of Xiaomi, noted earlier this year that some of the firm’s U.S. limited partners—the pensions, endowments and family offices that back U.S. VC firms—have been worried they’re missing out on a potential opportunity .

title: Anthropic in Talks for 1-Gigawatt Data Center Lease With Apollo-Backed Developer
content: Anthropic is in early talks to lease up to 1 gigawatt in compute capacity from a data center developer majority-owned by Apollo Global Management, part of a major effort by the AI company to reduce its reliance on cloud providers. The maker of Claude has discussed signing on as a direct tenant of sites developed by Stream Data Centers, a 27-year-old company with facilities across the U.S., and filling them with tensor processing units designed by Broadcom and Google, according to people with knowledge of the discussions. Anthropic has also discussed the possibility of Google providing a credit guarantee for the project, some of the people said. It’s not clear what part of the project it would backstop. Anthropic has previously sought a Google backstop for other data center leases, The Information has reported . Anthropic could also house other AI chips in the facilities, such as Nvidia’s graphics processing units, one of these people said. Nvidia has been making significant investments in a variety of projects and data center–related firms to ensure that its chips, rather than TPUs, end up in major facilities powering advanced AI. Either way, a gigawatt of computing capacity would require a capital investment of at least $40 billion, data center developers say. Anthropic currently secures the vast majority of its computing capacity by renting chip servers from cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services, Google and SpaceX. Anthropic has already agreed to lease smaller facilities run by former bitcoin miners Hut 8 and TeraWulf, giving it direct control over data center servers and opening a path to cut its compute costs by circumventing the cloud providers, which are seeking their own profits. The Stream arrangement could end up as its biggest lease deal so far and comes as archrival OpenAI has been pursuing a similar strategy. An agreement with Stream is still months away from completion and could still fall apart, the people said. The exact capacity Anthropic may seek is still under discussion, and it was not immediately clear exactly how the parties would structure the transaction. But Anthropic would need financial guarantees for the data center leases and financing for the chips going into the facilities, the people familiar with the discussions said. Along with leasing data centers, Anthropic has also started to lease chips directly from providers. Earlier this year, it announced a deal with AMD for 2 GW worth of chips. It has also entered into a $35 billion agreement to lease TPUs from a special purpose vehicle set up by Apollo and Blackstone. That partnership could expand: Broadcom has said it wants to work with the financial firms to finance more than 20 GW of compute, suggesting a combined $700 billion in chip purchases. Anthropic is competing with OpenAI to secure compute contracts. However, a finite number of data center developers have lined up the power supplies and permits necessary for facilities. For instance, OpenAI last month agreed to lease the first phase of a planned 10 GW data center in Ohio with credit support from Nvidia covering up to $105 billion. The project is attractive in part because the site sits on federal land and has U.S. government support. Anthropic, meanwhile, has entered into $531 billion worth of compute deals in just the last 11 months, largely with cloud providers such as AWS, Google and Microsoft. Unlike renting servers from big cloud operators, leasing data centers usually involves purchasing and operating the server equipment they house. That could eventually give Anthropic and OpenAI more control over chip price and supply, as well as related technology like server racks and networking equipment. At the same time, the companies would take on the financial burden of obtaining the costly equipment and hiring the people to manage it. Anthropic is hiring dozens of workers, including some in Canada and Australia, for roles such as securing power and working on facility design and structure. Dallas-based Stream Data Centers has developed more than 20 data center sites in the U.S. Apollo bought a majority stake in the company last year; Principal Asset Management also owns a stake.

title: AI, the UN, Xi and Trump
content: It’s a big week for global leaders talking about AI. We’ve got a bunch of presidents and prime ministers at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York—motorcades are creating chaos in Midtown Manhattan right now—and Chinese president Xi Jinping is due to arrive in Washington tomorrow. The top executives from most big tech firms will be at a state dinner on Thursday night with Xi, while some will also be at the U.N. earlier in the week. You can bet AI will dominate much of the discussion both at the U.N. and in Washington. It’s unlikely anything of substance will emerge, although there’ll be plenty of breathless headlines. On Tuesday morning, for instance, President Donald Trump made news by pronouncing that artificial intelligence would henceforth be known as super intelligence in U.S. government paperwork, because the word “artificial” makes AI sound “fake.” (See below for more on this.) Glad to see the leader of the free world is staying on top of the most important issues! Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham was reported to be planning to insert his country into the AI regulatory debate by claiming the U.K. could play the “honest broker” in AI governance. Cute. Otherwise, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is due to speak to the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday. The ChatGPT firm on Monday outlined the need for “international efforts to develop standards” for AI safety, so Altman will presumably elaborate on that. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is reportedly also speaking to the U.N. Security Council. The real action, though, may be in Washington, when Xi and Trump meet. Maybe they’ll discuss some way of working together to address AI safety, as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday officials from both sides had discussed. Xi, meanwhile, may be feeling a little irritated that Anthropic has accused some of China’s best-known AI firms of using Anthropic’s Claude illicitly—and in some cases routing sensitive Chinese data to Claude. That prompted China’s internet regulator to investigate DeepSeek and Moonshot AI over possibly breaching Chinese data security rules, we scooped today . Could this be why Xi, according to The Wall Street Journal , isn’t expected to bring corporate executives with him? As this U.S.-China expert explained in a post on X today, the “fraught relationship” between Chinese AI companies and the Chinese government is a hugely undercovered story. Super v. Artificial? Did Ilya Sutskever just win the lottery? Trump’s declaration that he was changing the name of artificial intelligence to superintelligence—SI instead of AI—could be great news for Sutskever’s AI startup, Safe Superintelligence Inc., or SSI . If Trump succeeds in replacing the AI term with SI, Sutskever’s company has the perfect brand. Sutskever might be even better off than Meta Platforms, whose CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, seems to be thinking along the same lines as Trump. Zuckerberg likes to talk about personal superintelligence , and his AI unit is called Meta Superintelligence Labs. (What’s the bet that most people prefer their super intelligence to be safe rather than personal?) Still, neither Sutskever nor Zuckerberg should celebrate yet. While Trump might be able to persuade Apple and Google to partially adopt the Lake America name in place of Lake Ontario, it’s hard to see anyone listening to him on AI. That term is just too ingrained in the culture right now. So while Trump’s decree might work for U.S. government paperwork, that’s probably as far as it goes. title: Barrick Gold Inks Five-Year AI Deal Before IPO
content: AI is top of mind for stock investors these days. That means even companies outside tech are beefing up their AI credentials ahead of new listings. In one such example, Barrick Gold’s North American unit has agreed to a five-year partnership with Avathon, a startup that develops AI-powered software to help industrial companies predict when expensive equipment will fail and monitors mine and factories sites for safety risks, Avathon CEO Pervinder Johar told me. Barrick is planning to float a minority stake in its North American unit, which produces the majority of its gold. The company has targeted year-end for the listing. The Barrick agreement is a windfall for 14-year-old Avathon. The miner will generate between $10 million to $20 million a year in sales for Avathon—about 10% of the Pleasanton, Calif.-based startup’s expected revenue next year, according to a person with direct knowledge of the discussions. Avathon’s annual recurring revenue recently rose to more than $50 million from about $15 million last year, the person said. In three years, Barrick’s North American unit could become Avathon’s second-largest customer, behind Aramco Digital, the tech arm of Saudi oil giant Aramco. Other large Avathon customers include Boeing, which owns 9% of the company, Airbus and the Department of Defense. Helped by these sales gains, Avathon is preparing to raise more than $100 million by the end of the year, the person with direct knowledge said. The startup was valued at $1.4 billion in January 2022. “This partnership is the tangible proof of physical AI moving beyond initial industry announcements to practical applications in extraction, energy and raw materials,” Johar said. Avathon’s software runs on about 200 AI models that help it map a company’s operations, monitoring what's happening through cameras and sensors and deciding how to handle changes. Barrick will pay a base fee to use Avathon’s platform, plus fees tied to the results it gets. Avathon’s software will scan footage from Barrick’s mine cameras to flag safety violations as they happen, and its AI agents will help Barrick buy supplies and negotiate supplier contracts, Johar said. And it will analyze Barrick's equipment to predict failures and recommend how to repair machines to keep them running longer. Avathon and Barrick started working together in December, and the software has been running at some U.S. sites, including the giant Nevada Gold Mines complex, since the second quarter. The rollout there is expected to be completed over the next couple of quarters. The next site will be in the Dominican Republic, Johar said. The Barrick deal follows Avathon's three-year partnership with Aramco Digital that was announced earlier this month. Aramco Digital plans to use Avathon’s software to make the towns Aramco built for its oil workers run more efficiently, with electricity meters and billing systems that run automatically. In addition, Aramco chose Avathon because it believes it will speed up its internal system tracking access and approvals, as well as supply chain logistics, equipment performance monitoring and the safety and compliance checks, said Raj Rao, chief growth officer at Aramco Digital. Avathon’s deals add to a recent wave of AI sales to industrial customers. Earlier this month, equipment maker Caterpillar and robotics startup FieldAI said they would bring autonomous machines to mining and construction sites. In May, robotics startup Humanoid said it would place humanoid robots at factories run by German industrial supplier Schaeffler. And in January, Hyundai and Boston Dynamics unveiled a production version of the Atlas humanoid robot, which Hyundai plans to put in its plants by 2028. title: Wall Street’s GPU Futures Push Stalls at the CFTC
content: The launch of futures for rental prices on Nvidia GPUs, which are seen as important to make AI compute an investable asset class, is hitting a snag. CME Group had hoped to launch contracts as soon as early October, but it won’t have regulatory approval by then. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates the futures market, is extending its review as it digs into how such contracts work and seeks comments from the broader industry, according to a letter to the exchange seen by The Information. In theory, such futures coupled with a liquid market to trade them could let AI companies and compute providers lock in prices for computing power ahead of time, helping them hedge against swings in GPU rental costs. Futures could also provide lenders behind the AI infrastructure financing boom with a way to hedge against the risk of GPUs used as collateral losing value. CME had announced last month it was aiming to launch compute futures on Oct. 5, pending regulatory approval. The firm would use a benchmark from startup data provider Silicon Data. It planned to start with two new futures products, one based on rental pricing for Nvidia H100s and another for Nvidia’s B200 chips. But later in August, the CFTC announced a broad request for comment on compute derivatives contracts, seeking to understand potential market manipulation among other risks. The CFTC noted that while a financial market for compute could support U.S. AI development, the underlying market is fragmented and opaque. For instance, GPU rental prices are typically set in bespoke private contracts as opposed to a big, open market. That raises the prospect that dominant players could influence market prices to their advantage. At the time, the CFTC opened a 60-day comment period to give market participants an opportunity to weigh in on the products. While that action raised doubts about the CME Group’s ability to meet its October timeline, the CFTC’s Sept. 21 letter confirms that the launch won’t go ahead next month. The CFTC noted that it needed more time to assess the CME launch “in light of novel or complex” issues, and would extend the review period on the products 45 days, until Nov. 9. In addition to CME, rival exchange firm Intercontinental Exchange has announced plans to launch GPU futures, but hasn’t set a specific date. Upstart exchanges too are vying to offer similar contracts. “We view additional regulatory review as a natural part of building a new derivatives market,” Carmen Li, CEO of Silicon Data, said in an emailed statement. “So whether the first contracts launch in October or somewhat later doesn’t change the underlying thesis. As more capital flows into AI infrastructure, the need for reliable compute pricing and tools to manage compute price risk is only becoming more important.” CME Group declined to comment.

title: New Data Show Anthropic, OpenAI and Other Upstarts Are Eating into Software Budgets
content: We’ve been reporting for months about how companies are shifting some traditional software spending to Anthropic and OpenAI. New data from procurement software firm Zip provides further evidence. AI providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, and Sierra accounted for 8% of spending by Zip customers in the 12 months that ended in August, up from 1.4% during the previous 12 months. Overall, their software budgets rose by a median of 13% during that period. The dozens of customers included in the study had an average of 2,400 employees and spent $18 billion for software, including AI, over the past four years. Zip’s customers include Snowflake, OpenAI, Datadog, Cloudflare and AMD. The shift is putting pressure on legacy software vendors to step up their game. Several enterprise software firms such as Workday and HubSpot as well as cloud providers Microsoft and Amazon are offering discounts or free trials of AI products to retain customers, we reported today . But just as the older companies are dangling those freebies, they’re also introducing more costly pricing models that charge customers for how much AI they use, rather than giving them unlimited AI as part of their subscriptions. Once the freebies end, some companies may decide the tools aren’t worth the hassle. Usage-Based Costs Rising With the shift to usage-based pricing, some customers are still seeing their bills rise, despite some discounts. This summer, for instance, spending by software provider Pegasystems on Microsoft’s Github Copilot, an AI coding tool, surged to $260,000 monthly from $20,000 after Microsoft shifted to usage-based pricing for the tool . “What I find really frustrating is [AI providers] put so much burden on companies, people like us, to detangle…what is the right way to use these” in a cost effective way, said David Vidoni, Pega’s chief information officer. (Pegasystems, which helps banks and telecoms to automate fraud detection and customer billing issues, spends between $10 million and $15 million annually on software, including AI.) After executives at Pegasystems balked, Microsoft offered the company one million credits worth $10,000 to use another tool, Copilot Cowork, an AI assistant akin to Claude Cowork, for one month. But that’s relatively piddly compared to the financial incentives Microsoft has given to other customers, our story today showed. But the financial incentive might work: Vidoni plans to expand testing of Copilot Cowork in his finance and marketing teams. Meanwhile, he is finding ways to cut costs linked to Github Copilot and other AI tools through employee spending caps and other methods. (Pega uses a variety of Microsoft tools beyond Github Copilot that could also make switching harder, though it does not run any customer-facing software products on Azure.) title: Why America’s AI Dream Is Failing to Launch
content: In 2022, American dominance in AI looked almost unassailable. The U.S. led in advanced models, semiconductors, capital and talent. Its closest competitor, China, appeared to be reeling from export controls that cut it off from the world’s most advanced process nodes, chips and memory technologies. Four years later, the tide seems to be turning. Chinese models have gained major global token share ; American technology giants are eyeing Chinese logic and memory chips ; and America’s grand AI ambitions face growing public backlash. During the first three months of 2026, local opposition blocked or delayed roughly $130 billion in data center projects. This spring, 71% of Americans surveyed opposed the construction of a data center near where they live. Texas, the fastest-growing state in data center construction, has frozen new grid-connected projects until further impact studies are completed. Data centers have become a bipartisan sleeper issue for the election cycle. Meanwhile, American leaders appear disconnected from voters whose consent they ultimately require to build. As frontier labs prepare for initial public offerings and President Donald Trump urges communities to “let Data Reign,” firmwide AI adoption and visible productivity gains remain limited . America’s problem is not a shortage of capital, chips or technical talent. It is the absence of an AI strategy that connects frontier capability to broadly shared economic gains, public legitimacy and the energy infrastructure required to deploy it. We write as an energy-compute analyst and a researcher focused on China’s AI policy. From the vantage points of the bottlenecks America’s physical AI build-out currently faces and China’s multifaceted approach to AI development, the U.S.’s huge capital expenditures on AI mask a dire situation: The country is financing an industrial revolution most citizens currently want no part of. That could still change. It will not change on the present terms. The American AI Dream(s) In the U.S.’s clearest articulation of AI priorities to date, America’s AI Action Plan focuses simply on “winning the race.” Policymakers are seeking to establish the U.S. AI stack as the “gold standard for AI worldwide,” though relevant measures of victory remain unclear. Advocates gesture toward job creation and higher standards of living but offer few tangible expectations for how Americans’ lives will improve. What, then, is the “American dream” for AI? Up to now, there have been two dominant versions. The first, from Silicon Valley, promises a world of infinite wealth and abundance achievable only through unprecedented investment in frontier labs and model training infrastructure. The cost of intelligence will fall so low that most forms of labor will no longer be required, freeing humans to bask in a life of leisure, intellectual curiosity and self-direction. The second, prevalent in Washington, is less a vision of what the dream is than what it cannot be : the nightmare of losing an arms race with China. These visions emerge from different institutional cultures but converge on the same message: the monopoly of power. In the former, Silicon Valley leaders are anchored by the economic belief that “ competition is for losers ” and the quasi-religious belief that whoever first creates the machine God will capture “ the light cone of all future value in the universe .” The latter vision treats AI principally as a tool for preserving American hegemony and fears apocalypse if that hegemony erodes. In short, you have visions for a techno utopia if we get our way and a techno dystopia if we don’t. Each works well within its respective echo chamber. Neither speaks persuasively to the lived experience of people outside these systems. For many Americans, the fundamental social compact—“if you work hard, you will be rewarded”—has been fractured by financial crises, wageless recoveries and a global pandemic. They have watched platform companies build business models linked to serious damage to children’s mental health . Now many of the same firms are asking to put a data center in their backyard. When labs pitch a “post-labor” economy, workers do not hear a promise of leisure; they hear consistent threats of a “ permanent underclass .” After repeated broken promises that technology would universally improve their lives, they have little reason to accept the claim that this time will be different. American leadership is promising either the moon or damnation. Americans are saying, “Prove it.” Four Orientations, Not One Compared to the U.S.’s fixation on frontier AI, China’s strategy is more multidimensional. Since 2020, Chinese leaders have organized science and technology policies around what Xi Jinping calls the “ Four Orientations ”: the technological frontier, economic development, major national needs, and the life and health of the people. The framework appears repeatedly in high-level AI policy and discourse, signaling what Beijing is optimizing for—and just as importantly, what goals it considers insufficient in isolation. China seeks frontier capabilities and has pursued legal and bureaucratic reforms intended to improve its innovation environment. But it has not treated frontier leadership as a singular AI strategy. That may have been out of necessity: Constrained in terms of advanced chips, computing power and capital, China needed a “ good enough ” strategy that balanced pragmatism with technological ambition. Yet the approach continued after the 2025 DeepSeek moment. Rather than treating frontier or frontier-adjacent model building as the sole national objective, Beijing continued to pursue industrial diffusion, technological sovereignty and governance alongside them. Economic development is arguably where much of Beijing’s policy attention lies. The “ AI Plus ” initiative, reiterated and expanded in 2025, has little to do with superintelligence. It sets industrial targets, directing local governments and firms toward productivity gains and industrial upgrades. The third orientation focuses on building secure core technological supply chains. After the first Trump administration’s 2019 campaign against Huawei, Xi told Chinese scientists and engineers that core technologies could not be “ borrowed, bought or begged for, ” but must be secured through domestic innovation. Chinese officials and bureaucrats subsequently intensified efforts to localize key parts of the semiconductor supply chain. China’s recent chip gains reflect in part the experimentation and investments this push set in motion. The fourth orientation mandates that tech development has to improve both public well-being and quality of life. In the post-ChatGPT period, governance has remained a formal policy priority . As concerns about automation and job displacement grew, the State Council incorporated research and preparation for those risks into high-level planning, while regulators strengthened accountability requirements for workers managed by algorithmic systems. When AI companions came under scrutiny for harms they caused to young people and vulnerable users, China’s cyberspace regulator moved quickly to finalize some of the world’s most stringent rules . While the government’s record on AI governance is far from perfect, and not all four orientations are equally transferable to the U.S., Beijing’s framework treats industrial development, sovereignty and governance as concurrent objectives rather than subordinating each to frontier competition. That contrast warrants reflection. A Race Is Not a Strategy China’s example shows that inclusive AI policy cannot consist merely of restricting competitors and accelerating domestic firms. A technology capable of creating significant economic gains, while imposing real social and physical costs, requires planning, coordination and harmonizing  of competing goals. For all of America’s advantages—and they are considerable—the U.S. faces substantial execution risk. The world’s best chips are of little use if developers cannot permit facilities to house them or build the generation capacity to power them. Nor should AI dominance be pursued in isolation. It may conflict with openness, safety, privacy, labor protections and international restraint. A credible American AI dream cannot be solely defined by winning an ambiguously defined race: It must be measured by whether ordinary Americans gain capability, security, opportunity and genuine freedom, including from avoidable technological harm. The U.S. needs a more holistic, pro-social definition for its AI dream. This is not anti-innovation; this is antifragile. Domestically, it means transparently incorporating local feedback into infrastructure planning, preparing workers for disruption rather than treating displacement as an abstraction, and giving the public concrete reasons to believe AI’s gains will be broadly shared. Globally, it means engaging constructively with partners and competitors, including China, to establish a shared account of AI’s most desirable outcomes and a common framework for managing its most consequential risks. If the U.S. wants its promise of AI-enabled abundance to survive contact with voters, it needs a pragmatic and inclusive strategy fast—or its dream will die on the launchpad.

title: Luckey’s Erebor Bank Plots Syria Expansion
content: Erebor Bank, fresh from becoming a vital new financial bridge between the U.S. and Venezuela, is eyeing a new foreign foray: expanding into Syria. The bank, founded by Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, has told staff and some investors it could help the war-torn Middle Eastern country reconnect to the global financial system, potentially attracting billions in deposits from businesses and consumers, according to people familiar with the strategy. Doing so would make Erebor a remarkably early mover in Syria, given that Washington only recently reopened the country to U.S. firms and investment. The potential Syria opportunity comes after a dramatic shift in U.S. relations with the country over the past couple years. President Donald Trump last year signaled his intention to remove sanctions on Syria after former dictator Bashar al-Assad was overthrown in 2024, ending his family’s decadeslong rule. The U.S. removed comprehensive sanctions last year and this August dropped Syria from the U.S. State Sponsors of Terrorism List, the last remaining major economic and financial penalty imposed on the country. Though it’s now legal for U.S. banks to do business in Syria, most large financial institutions remain wary of entering the country, in part because they’re worried about heightened risks of exposure to activities like money laundering and terrorism financing. Erebor, part of a new cohort of banks that has received charters under the Trump administration, has from the start been willing to enter businesses most larger banks avoid, particularly when doing so aligns with U.S. government goals. In recent months, Erebor Chair Jacob Hirshman has traveled to Syria to meet with business and government officials interested in rebuilding the country’s economy, the people said. Luckey, meanwhile, recently told staff at a companywide meeting that Erebor was working toward playing its own part in reconnecting Syria to the global financial system, emphasizing that the bank was interested in supporting U.S. foreign policy, according to people familiar with the remarks. Erebor, which has emphasized its U.S. government ties to investors and is nearing a $1.5 billion fundraise at an $8 billion valuation, has already gained traction in areas prioritized by the Trump administration, such as defense startups and cryptocurrency firms . It is also serving as an intermediary for companies seeking loans from the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital, according to people briefed on the matter. Luckey, who backed the bank along with Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz, has said he helped launch Erebor to fill a gap in the market. “I realized that you didn’t have banks that were aligned with the U.S.’s interests,” Luckey told TBPN. And Luckey, in the all-company meeting, highlighted opportunities for the bank beyond Syria that are currently off-limits but could open up as the geopolitical situation changes. He said Erebor could possibly even eventually supply financial services to places such as Cuba as well as North Korea, where Luckey said he believes the Trump administration could broker a peace deal permitting North Korea to keep its nuclear weapons. Some Western financial institutions have been making inroads to restore financial services in Syria in recent weeks. Mastercard launched the country’s first internationally accepted payment card in partnership with Qatari bank QNB Group, and Visa processed Syria’s first international card payments in more than 15 years. Though talks about how Erebor will support investors and businesses in Syria are still in the early stages, an expansion of its efforts there could mirror the bank’s support of U.S. goals and business interests in Venezuela following the U.S. ouster of President Nicolás Maduro. Earlier this year, Erebor entered Venezuela as the country reconnected to the U.S. financial system following years of sanctions and the Trump administration moved to revive its oil sector. Erebor now has banking relationships with Venezuela’s central bank and commercial banks and is facilitating transactions for companies, including U.S. oil firms investing in the region. Erebor could play a similar role in Syria for energy companies such as Chevron and Baker Hughes that are looking to explore and develop Syria’s oil and gas fields. Hirshman traveled to Syria in July to explore potential options for collaborations with the central bank and firms operating in the country, according to people familiar with the matter. This month, Erebor was among roughly 50 U.S. companies that sent representatives to Damascus with an American Chamber of Commerce delegation, according to a list published by the Syrian Foreign Ministry. U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Jacob McGee urged the delegation to invest in Syria, noting companies including Chevron, Mastercard and Visa were already taking steps in that direction, according to local news reports. Still, reconnecting Syria to the global financial system could be more difficult than helping companies and investment firms enter Venezuela. Years of sanctions and civil war have left most of the Syrian population below the poverty line and without banking services. They must conduct most daily transactions in cash. Many Western banks remain wary of processing transactions in the country, limiting services like cross-border payments and trade finance. A handbook issued by the U.S. embassy in Syria for potential investors into Syria notes that many international banks’ risk-averse approach to processing U.S. dollar transactions could lead to lengthy due diligence, delays and refusals.

title: The Download: India’s smart glasses menace and AI’s trillion-dollar gamble
content:
The Download: India’s smart glasses menace and AI’s trillion-dollar gamble
Plus: hackers claim they've stolen data on almost all FBI employees.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India
When Shubnam saw an Instagram video of a Delhi protest they had attended, they realized a content creator wearing Meta smart glasses had recorded them surreptitiously. The mocking reel drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse and AI-generated memes.
Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream. The risks are particularly acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive.
The bigger issue is that the smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also becoming a tool of police surveillance.
Here’s why smart glasses are creating new privacy risks in India.
—Anuj Behal
MIT Technology Review Narrated: what’s at stake in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble
When Jessica Wachter, a University of Pennsylvania finance professor, wanted to assess AI’s impact on the economy over the next few years, she started with a simple fact: a handful of so-called hyperscalers are investing huge amounts of money to build AI data centers.
Instead of trying to predict how widely deployed AI models will be, Wachter asked how fast the hyperscalers’ earnings will need to grow to justify their spending through 2027, when expenditures are expected to reach nearly $1.1 trillion.
The results are eye-opening. AI companies will need to achieve an extraordinary increase in productivity just to break even by 2030.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

title: Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Shubnam was packing boxes for a move into a new home when their friend sent them an Instagram video. The footage had only been up for a few hours, but it was days old, recorded at a Delhi protest this spring against a bill that would have narrowed the legal recognition for transgender people in India.
There, a content creator known for rage-bait videos had approached Shubnam, a 38-year-old transfeminine graphic designer and educator. Shubnam, who uses a single chosen name, was dressed in a green sari with a shaved head, and the creator asked why they were wearing “female clothing.” Shubnam told him to back off. Only when the video arrived did they realize he had recorded the exchange on Meta smart glasses, styled to look like ordinary Wayfarers.
Edited into a mocking reel, the footage drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse, reaction videos, and AI-generated memes. It spread from Instagram to X and YouTube. Copies remain online today.
For Shubnam, the video has caused huge harm. “All it took was one unconsented video to rewind two decades of progress that I made all on my own,” they told
MIT Technology Review
. “For a moment, it felt like this entire adult life I had lived was just a long lucid dream, and I was going to wake up as that clueless queer child again.” They haven’t worn a sari outside their neighborhood since.
Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream. And they say privacy problems are becoming especially acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive.
of cyberstalking, sextortion, deepfakes, and other forms of online abuse are growing in the country. And the chances of a crackdown on technologies such as smart glasses are slim, given that Indian law enforcement authorities are themselves increasingly adopting AI-powered surveillance tools, including facial recognition systems and their own AI-enabled smart glasses.
An unequal burden
Smart glasses are among the fastest-growing devices in India’s wearables market, according to the
International Data Corporation
, a research firm. And Reliance Jio, one of the country’s largest telecommunications companies, says that later this year it’s
launch a sub-$105 rival to Meta’s glasses, the latest model of which have a $420 price tag in India.
The core privacy issue is that these cameras don’t look like cameras, so targets may not notice they’re being recorded. Yet Meta rejects the idea that it’s responsible for protecting people from intrusions, says Janusz Świerczyński, an Oxford Saïd Business School researcher who studies privacy and emerging technology.
“More and more, the expectation is being placed on bystanders to look out for themselves,” he says. That means it’s up to them to spot a small LED in the glasses frames that activates when recording is in progress. Meta also relies on wearers to behave responsibly, says Świerczyński. Reliance Jio did not respond to our request for comment on privacy issues related to its upcoming glasses.
Creators have already demonstrated ways to circumvent the recording light on Meta’s glasses. Tutorials show users how to cover or otherwise obscure the LED while continuing to record. Back in March,
documented a market for “stealth mode” modifications that physically disable the light or remove it entirely.
All that makes covert recording easier, and the risks are not borne equally. Świerczyński says women and other marginalized groups face greater harm when inconspicuous devices capture and circulate footage without consent—as happened to Shubnam.
The bigger problem, however, is that in India smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also being adopted as a tool of police surveillance.
In June, when thousands of young demonstrators gathered to protest problems with the country’s education system, Delhi police used
Meta smart glasses
to record them. In fact, a petition filed by former Jawaharlal Nehru University Students’ Union president Aishe Ghosh before the Delhi High Court alleged that police had filmed protesters continuously for weeks, including while they were eating and resting. It also alleged that the police had threatened to send footage of student demonstrators to their parents and colleges.
In July, India’s solicitor general dismissed the case in court as “
luxury litigation.
” Instead of investigating the students’ complaints, police turned on the students themselves,
opening 10 criminal investigations
for offenses including rioting, assault on public servants, and damage to public property. Some of the protesters, who spoke to
MIT Technology Review
on condition of anonymity, say they never saw the LED on the Meta AI glasses police wore during the demonstrations.
Filming without consent
Meta maintains that its safeguard works. The company told
MIT Technology Review
, “Every pair has a capture LED that blinks when you take a photo or video that you can save or share; it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or damages the LED, the camera is disabled.” The company also says users are responsible for complying with the law and respecting people’s privacy.
That approach is risky, especially in India, where norms around filming and consent are still highly disputed and digital literacy is still uneven, says Sameer Parmar, a counselor at Meri Trustline, a safety partner working with Meta and YouTube to support people harmed by online content.
“The hardware is improving, but the country’s weak understanding of consent gives an invisible camera far more room to cause harm,” he says. Simply being in a public place is often treated as implicit consent to be photographed or filmed. He says the help line has been seeing an uptick in cases involving covert recording and nonconsensual footage.
“Violations of this access have increased significantly and are expected to rise further in India,” he says. People are recorded in medical settings, during private encounters, and in public spaces. Those with less power to object are particularly vulnerable, he adds.
“It’s either trolling or it’s playing pranks on them and then recording them” he says. Abusers “do target people who are a little more unaware or susceptible to how this technology-facilitated harm works.”
The law in India has not caught up with this new kind of harm, says Apar Gupta, a lawyer and founder-director of the Internet Freedom Foundation. “India’s laws against voyeurism and the sharing of intimate images were designed largely around more recognizable forms of abuse,” he says, citing offenses such as secretly filming someone undressing, using a toilet, or engaged in a sexual act. “[The laws] offer limited protection when someone is secretly filmed in an ordinary public setting and the footage is then used to humiliate them,” he says.
Social media platforms’ rules do offer another route to removing harmful content filmed with smart glasses, but it’s not an immediate remedy. “Under India’s current rules, platforms can have up to 36 hours to act on certain complaints—a window that can be long enough for a video to be downloaded, copied, and circulated elsewhere,” he says.
The problem of filming without consent seems set to grow. According to the
Financial Times
, some internal prototypes of new Meta glasses include AI features that continuously photograph and listen to the wearer’s surroundings, enabling the glasses to later recall what they saw or heard. These functions wouldn’t activate the external recording indicator, making it impossible for bystanders to know when information about them is being collected.
Meta told us it intends to keep the LED for active capture, such as taking photos or recording video, but not for AI features that interpret the wearer’s surroundings. Its argument is that a constantly blinking light could eventually become so commonplace that people stop noticing it.
But that logic risks putting society in a perpetual game of catch-up, says Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law at Boston University. “Tech companies have an incredible ability to push these tools out faster than society can meaningfully acclimate to the threat,” he says. “By the time society catches up, there’s already a degree of normalization.”
For Shubnam, the danger is not just that people may become accustomed to being recorded. It is that they will become accustomed to seeing versions of themselves that they never chose to put out into the world.
“Being comprehended along the lines of a narrative that I didn’t compose or consent to—that imposed recognition makes you feel like you’re powerless in how people know you,” they say.

Der Siegener Professor im Ruhestand Prof. Dr.-Ing. Mario Pacas erhält eine der wichtigsten Auszeichnungen der IEEE Power Electronics Society (PELS). Gewürdigt werden seine langjährigen Verdienste um die internationale Zusammenarbeit sowie sein Einsatz für die stärkere Präsenz der Fachgesellschaft in Europa und Lateinamerika.
Für seine Verdienste ist Prof. Dr.-Ing. Mario Pacas mit dem „Harry A. Owen, Jr. Distinguished Service Award“ ausgezeichnet worden. Die Ehrung wurde er von der internationalen Fachgesellschaft für Leistungselektronik IEEE-PELS (IEEE Power Electronics Society) vorgenommen. IEEE ist eine der bedeutendsten Organisationen für Fachleute aus Elektrotechnik, Elektronik, Informatik und verwandten technischen Disziplinen. Sie bringt Forschende, Ingenieurinnen und Ingenieure sowie Fachleute aus Hochschulen und Industrie zusammen und fördert den Austausch über neue Technologien und Forschungsergebnisse. PELS ist die Fachgesellschaft innerhalb von IEEE, die sich den Themen der Leistungselektronik widmet. Pacas war über viele Jahre in verschiedenen Funktionen für die Fachgesellschaft tätig und setzte sich dabei für ihre internationale Vernetzung ein.
Pacas war von 1996 bis 2024 Professor für Elektrotechnik an der Universität Siegen und Inhaber des Lehrstuhls für Leistungselektronik und elektrische Antriebe. Er verband Forschung und Lehre stets mit einem ausgeprägten internationalen Engagement. Die Auszeichnung würdigt sein Wirken für die Fachgesellschaft und die Weiterentwicklung der Leistungselektronik. Zugleich unterstreicht sie die internationale Sichtbarkeit der Arbeit, die Pacas während seiner Tätigkeit an der Universität Siegen geleistet hat.
Seine berufliche Laufbahn begann Pacas nach dem Studium der Elektrotechnik an der Universität Karlsruhe und der Promotion im Jahr 1985 in der Industrie. Von 1985 bis 1996 arbeitete er bei BBC/ABB in der Schweiz und in Deutschland in verschiedenen Forschungs-, Entwicklungs- und Leitungsfunktionen. Dabei sammelte er umfangreiche Erfahrungen in internationalen Projekten. Unter anderem war er für die Entwicklung von Servoantrieben verantwortlich.
Heute ist der emeritierte Professor weiterhin als unabhängiger Berater in den Bereichen Leistungselektronik, elektrische Antriebe und Automatisierung tätig. Er ist außerdem Mitglied vom Wissenschaftlichen Beirat (Editorial Board) renommierter Fachzeitschriften auf dem Gebiet der Elektrotechnik.

Brände verhindern, Risiken erkennen und Leben schützen: Bereits seit 1987 treffen sich in Braunschweig Fachleute, die sich dieser anspruchsvollen Aufgabe verschrieben haben. Zum 40. Jubiläum der Braunschweiger Brandschutz-Tage kommen vom 30. September bis 1. Oktober 2026 im Audimax der Technischen Universität Braunschweig erneut Expert*innen aus Wissenschaft, Behörden und Praxis – darunter Feuerwehren, Ingenieurbüros und Versicherungen – zusammen, um über aktuelle Entwicklungen eines sich wandelnden Bauwesens zu diskutieren. Ein Schwerpunkt liegt in diesem Jahr auf Lösungen für Bestandsgebäude und deren Umnutzung sowie neuen Brandschutzvorschriften.
„Sicherheit ist eine zentrale gesellschaftliche Aufgabe und wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse sind eine wichtige Grundlage, um sie zu gewährleisten. Die Braunschweiger Brandschutz-Tage leisten seit vier Jahrzehnten einen wertvollen Beitrag dazu. Dieses Jubiläum steht für eine Erfolgsgeschichte, auf die wir als Universität sehr stolz sind“, sagt die Präsidentin der TU Braunschweig, Professorin Angela Ittel.
„Guter Brandschutz schützt Leben – und er muss zugleich mit den Veränderungen beim Bauen Schritt halten. Wenn wir bestehende Gebäude anders nutzen, mehr mit Holz bauen oder neue Energie- und Gebäudetechnik einsetzen, brauchen wir Lösungen, die Sicherheit und Innovation zusammenbringen. Genau dafür ist der Austausch zwischen Wissenschaft, Behörden und Praxis so wichtig. Die Braunschweiger Brandschutz-Tage leisten diesen Wissenstransfer seit 40 Jahren. Das ist eine beeindruckende Erfolgsgeschichte aus Niedersachsen mit Wirkung weit über die Landesgrenzen hinaus“, sagt Niedersachsens Wirtschafts- und Bauminister Grant Hendrik Tonne.
Von der Forschung in die Praxis
Als 1987 die erste Tagung unter Leitung von Professor Dietmar Hosser stattfand, war Brandschutz noch keine eigenständige Fachdisziplin und die ersten Brandschutzbüros waren gerade in Gründung. Der verheerende Brand am Düsseldorfer Flughafen im Jahr 1996, bei dem 17 Menschen starben, war eine Zäsur. Seitdem hat sich der Brandschutz erheblich professionalisiert. So kamen unter anderem neue Regelungen zu Rauchmeldern, Sprinkleranlagen und Rettungswegen hinzu. Heute stellen nachhaltige Baustoffe, innovative Energietechnik, intelligente Gebäudesysteme und veränderte Nutzungen die Fachleute vor neue Aufgaben.
„Ein Markenzeichen der Braunschweiger Brandschutz-Tage war schon damals – und ist es bis heute geblieben – Inhalte aus der Forschung in die Praxis zu übertragen,“ sagt Professor Jochen Zehfuß, wissenschaftlicher Tagungsleiter und Leiter des Fachgebiets Brandschutz im Institut für Baustoffe, Massivbau und Brandschutz (iBMB) der TU Braunschweig. „Die vergangenen 40 Jahre haben gezeigt, wie wichtig dieser ständige Austausch für die Weiterentwicklung des Brandschutzes ist.“
Die Rekonstruktion der Brandkatastrophe in Crans-Montana
Neben dem Rückblick auf vier Jahrzehnte vorbeugenden Brandschutz stehen in diesem Jahr der Holzbau sowie Bestandsgebäude und deren Umnutzung im Zentrum der Tagung. So werden Brandschutzlösungen und -konzepte am Beispiel der Allianz Arena, einer zur Kulturstätte umgenutzten ehemaligen Werft in Lübeck und des großen ehemaligen Verlagsgebäudes am Baumwall in Hamburg vorgestellt.
Ein besonders eindrücklicher Programmpunkt widmet sich der Brandkatastrophe im schweizerischen Crans-Montana in der Silvesternacht 2025. In einem Vortrag wird das Ereignis rekonstruiert und die Untersuchungen zum Brandverlauf vorgestellt. „Hier wird gezeigt, welche verheerenden Auswirkungen es haben kann, wenn Vorschriften nicht eingehalten werden“, so Professor Zehfuß.
Darüber hinaus präsentieren Expert*innen Erkenntnisse darüber, wann Fehlalarme auftreten und wie diese vermieden werden können. Ein weiteres Thema sind die Wechselwirkungen von PV- und Rauchabzugsanlagen sowie wichtige Neuerungen im Vorschriftenbereich.
Einen weiteren Höhepunkt bildet die Verleihung des bundesweit einmaligen Brandschutz-Nachwuchspreises für herausragende studentische Arbeiten am 30. September.
Über die Brandschutz-Tage
Die „Braunschweiger Brandschutz-Tage“ zählen zu den bedeutendsten Brandschutz-Fachtagungen im deutschsprachigen Raum. Rund 500 im Brandschutz tätige Ingenieur*innen aus Bauaufsichtsbehörden, Feuerwehren, Versicherungen, Ingenieurbüros, Industrie, Prüfanstalten und Forschungseinrichtungen kommen auf Einladung des Instituts für Baustoffe, Massivbau und Brandschutz der TU Braunschweig einmal im Jahr zum Informations- und Gedankenaustausch zusammen.
